1.overview:
After Joshua’s death Israel asks the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites, and the answer is Judah. Judah and Simeon win at Bezek and cut off the thumbs and great toes of its king, Adoni-bezek, who admits he had done the same to seventy kings. Judah burns Jerusalem and takes Hebron and Debir, where Othniel wins Caleb’s daughter Achsah, and the house of Joseph takes Bethel after a man of the city shows them the way in. Then the report turns into a list of tribes that did not drive the Canaanites out.

The chapter runs downhill. It opens with the LORD’s promise to Judah and closes with Dan, the last tribe named, pushed back into the hills by the Amorites (v. 34). The wars of Joshua are over, and what is left is a land shared with the people Israel was meant to replace.

1.hermeneutics:
Maiming defeated enemies was open policy in the ancient world, and kings boasted of it. Ashurnasirpal II of Assyria (9th century BC) records that he cut off the hands and fingers of some captives and the noses and ears of others. The thumb had a military meaning: Aelian and Plutarch report an Athenian decree that prisoners of war lose the right thumb, so that they could still pull an oar but never again hold a spear. A man without thumbs and great toes cannot grip a weapon or stand firm in a fight, and seventy such kings gathering scraps under a table (v. 7) are living trophies of a court. What sets v. 7 apart is the speaker. Adoni-bezek himself calls the punishment fair, “as I have done, so God hath requited me,” and the narrator adds nothing.

Archaeology shows the same divide the chapter draws between hills and valleys. Around 1200 BC the number of settlements in the central hill country rose from about 25 to about 250, most of them farming villages with pillared “four-room” houses and collared-rim storage jars. The cities of the plains carried on. Beth-shean (v. 27) was an Egyptian administrative and garrison town, with stelae of Seti I and a monument of Ramesses II, until it burned about 1150 BC, and Megiddo kept its Canaanite culture for a long time after. Verse 19 states the result in one line: Judah held “the mountain” but not “the valley.” Read against that map, vv. 27–33 describe where the newcomers could settle and where they could not.

rows.text: Judah, with Simeon and Caleb: cities taken

notes: **Did not drive out:** the Hebrew verb for driving out (*yarash*) is negated nine times (vv. 19, 21, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33). Before that it is used only for success (vv. 19, 20).

**Who lives among whom:** first the Canaanites dwell among Israel (vv. 29–30), then Asher and Naphtali dwell among the Canaanites (vv. 32–33). Tribute (*mas*, vv. 28, 30, 33, 35) is the only gain left.
**Go up:** the verb comes six times in vv. 1–22, always for Israel advancing (vv. 1, 2, 3, 4, 16, 22). The next one to “come up” is the angel of 2:1.

Judges has two introductions. The first (1:1–2:5) begins “after the death of Joshua,” surveys the land tribe by tribe, and ends when the angel at Bochim explains why the Canaanites remain. The second (2:6–3:6) goes back to Joshua’s death and tells the same failure as a religious pattern. Much of ch. 1 repeats Joshua 15–19, now arranged as a record of what was left undone.
**Forward:** Dan’s failure (v. 34) prepares for its migration north in ch. 18, and the Jebusites of v. 21 hold Jerusalem until David takes the stronghold of Zion (2 Samuel 5:6–9).

traditions.text: A thematic link to Adoni-bezek’s confession that God repaid him in kind. Condemned to burn, Abinadi tells King Noah’s priests that what they do to him will come back on them, and that they will “suffer, as I suffer, the pains of death by fire.” Noah himself dies by fire at his own people’s hands (Mosiah 19:20). Mormon later notes that Abinadi’s words were fulfilled when the priests’ descendants were hunted and slain.

Josephus answers the question of v. 1 through a named priest: Phinehas prophesies that the government should go to the tribe of Judah. His Adonibezek confesses that he could not stay hidden from God forever, having done the same to seventy-two kings, and is carried alive to Jerusalem. Josephus also eases the tension between vv. 8 and 21: Judah took the lower city and killed its people, but the upper city was too strong to be taken.

This retelling moves from Joshua’s death to a new question put to God: shall we go up against the Philistines? God answers that they may go if their heart is pure, and the people first ask for a leader. The angel of the LORD has them cast lots on the tribe of Caleb, and the lot falls on Kenaz, who becomes ruler of Israel. Where Judges answers with a tribe, Pseudo-Philo answers with one man.

Rashi first gives the plain sense: v. 1 asks which tribe should go up into its allotted but unconquered land. He then reports a reading from Temurah in which “Judah” is a person, Othniel, whose real name was Judah, brother of Simeon. On that reading the question is who will lead, and the LORD names the man who becomes Israel’s first judge in 3:9. It meets Pseudo-Philo halfway, with Othniel in the place of Kenaz, whom Judges names as his father.

The Aramaic Targum of the Prophets adds a cause to v. 19. Judah drove out the people of the hills, it says, but could not drive out those of the plain after they had sinned. The iron chariots stay in the verse, but the reason moves from weapons to conduct, the same reason the angel gives at Bochim (2:2–3). Rashi quotes this rendering.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on Judges 1:19; Rashi on 1:19

traditions.text: The Talmud uses the Bethel story to show the reward for escorting a traveler. The man of vv. 24–25 neither spoke nor walked; Rabbi Yohanan says he only pointed with his finger, and for that he and his descendants were saved for all generations. A baraita adds that his new Luz (v. 26) was where blue wool was dyed, a town Sennacherib never exiled and Nebuchadnezzar never destroyed, and the angel of death may not pass through it.

The Greek text turns v. 18 into a failure: Judah did not take Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron or Ashdod. In v. 19 it also gives the valley a defender, saying Judah could not drive out its people because “Rechab prevented them,” apparently reading the Hebrew word for chariot (*rekev*) as a name. Josephus agrees that Gaza and Ekron escaped Judah, because they lay in flat country and had many chariots.

Reading the Greek, Augustine asks why Judah feared iron chariots if the LORD was with him. His answer is that the setback was itself a kindness. A people that took everything without a struggle would swell with pride, so God lets his own profit from fearing their enemies as well as from beating them, as Paul was given a thorn in the flesh “lest I should be exalted above measure” (2 Corinthians 12:7).

The Greek of v. 27 calls Beth-shean “a city of Scythians,” and Augustine notes that it is the city now called Scythopolis. How could Scythians found a town so far from home? He points to Alexander, who founded an Alexandria far from Macedonia, and to histories that tell of Scythians holding almost all of Asia when they marched against a king of Egypt.
traditions.cite: Questions on the Heptateuch 7.8; Judges 1:27 LXX

traditions.text: Eusebius lists Bezek as the city of Adoni-bezek and says that in his day two villages of that name stood near each other, seventeen miles from Neapolis (Shechem) on the road to Scythopolis. That places the first battle of the book in the northern hills, well outside Judah’s own lot, in the same region as the Bezek where Saul later numbered Israel (1 Samuel 11:8).

2.overview:
An angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and charges Israel with making leagues with the Canaanites and sparing their altars. The LORD will no longer drive the nations out; they will be thorns in Israel’s sides and their gods a snare. The people weep, name the place Bochim (“weepers”), and sacrifice. The story then steps back to Joshua’s death and burial and to a new generation “which knew not the LORD.” What follows is the plan of the whole book: Israel serves the Baals, the LORD sells them to plunderers, he raises up judges who rescue them, and when each judge dies they turn back worse than before.

The chapter tells the book’s pattern before any of its stories. Every later episode, from Othniel to Samson, is one turn of the cycle set out in vv. 11–19.

2.hermeneutics:
The Hebrew title *shophet*, “judge,” meant more than a man who heard lawsuits. At Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC) the *šāpiṭum* was a provincial governor. In the Ugaritic myths “judge” stands in parallel with “king” as a title of gods: Baal is called “our king” and “our judge,” and his rival, the sea god Yamm, is “Judge River.” Centuries later Carthage, a Phoenician colony, was headed by two *sufetes*, the same word, elected each year. When v. 16 says the LORD “raised up judges, which delivered them,” a first hearer would think of rulers and rescuers, not magistrates. The book uses the word that way: apart from Deborah (4:5), its judges are never shown deciding a case.

Verse 13 pairs Baal with the Ashtaroth, the plural of Ashtoreth, the goddess the Phoenicians called Astarte. In Akkadian the name of the goddess Ishtar had become a common noun for any goddess, and Assyrian texts can speak of “the gods and the ishtars,” meaning gods and goddesses. The Hebrew plurals work the same way. “Baalim” (v. 11) and “Ashtaroth” (v. 13) are less two named deities than the male and female gods of every town around Israel, “the gods of the people that were round about them” (v. 12). The charge is not that Israel traded the LORD for one rival but that it took up the whole local pantheon.

notes: **The motive:** v. 18 says the LORD acts because of “their groanings,” not because Israel repents. In the stories that follow, Israel “cried unto the LORD” (3:9, 15) before each deliverer is raised.
**Fathers:** the Hebrew word for “fathers” comes seven times (vv. 1, 10, 12, 17, 19, 20, 22). Each generation is measured against the one before, and in v. 19 it is worse.

**Covenant:** the same word, *berit*, is “my covenant” (v. 1), the “league” Israel was not to make (v. 2), and the covenant transgressed (v. 20). “Judge” appears six times in vv. 16–19 and nowhere earlier in the book.

Chapter 2 joins the book’s two introductions. Verses 1–5 close the first: Bochim answers the failures of ch. 1 with a word from the LORD. Verse 6 starts the second by going back to Joshua’s dismissal of the people (Joshua 24:28–31), and 2:11–3:6 set out the pattern every later story follows.

**Backward and forward:** the thorns of v. 3 come from Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13. Samuel’s farewell retells the cycle with names: Sisera, the Philistines and Moab, then Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel (1 Samuel 12:9–11).

traditions.text: Where the KJV says that it repented the LORD (v. 18), the Joseph Smith Translation, as the Church’s footnote shows, reads “for the Lord hearkened” because of their groanings. The same footnote gives the Hebrew sense as “to be sorry,” “moved to pity,” or “have compassion,” and points to Psalm 106:45. The change keeps what moves God in the verse, the cry of an oppressed people, without saying that God repented.

Mormon pauses in his record to lament the speed of the turn: “how quick to do iniquity, and how slow to do good,” how quick to be lifted up in pride and how slow to remember the Lord their God. The Church’s footnote to “turned quickly” in v. 17 points here. Judges tells the pattern as history; Mormon names the trait in people that drives it.

A thematic link. The Book of Mormon runs a whole cycle in a few years. At Nephi’s prayer the Lord sends famine in place of war, the people remember the Lord and repent, and peace returns; robbers then rise, and the people are stirred up again in remembrance. By the eighty-second year “they began again to forget the Lord their God,” the relapse of v. 19 in Nephite form.

Who was the angel of v. 1? Leviticus Rabbah answers Phinehas: prophets are called messengers, the same Hebrew word as angel, and when the holy spirit rested on Phinehas his face burned like a torch. Rashi gives the same answer from Seder Olam, and the Targum makes the messenger a prophet sent from before the LORD. Josephus, too, has Phinehas speak for God after Joshua’s death (Antiquities 5.2.1).
traditions.cite: Leviticus Rabbah 1:1; Rashi on Judges 2:1; Targum Jonathan on 2:1

traditions.text: The Greek has the angel go up from Gilgal “to the place of weeping, and to Bæthel,” and on to the house of Israel. Naming Bethel ties Bochim to the place where Israel later sits and weeps before the LORD (20:26; 21:2, where “house of God” is Bethel) and to the oak below Bethel called Allon-bachuth, “oak of weeping” (Genesis 35:8).

Josephus explains the rebuke by prosperity. After Bethel, he says, the Israelites gave up war for farming, grew rich and soft, and stopped attending to their laws; God was angry and reminded them that they had spared the Canaanites against his orders. They grieved but still would not fight, and living on Canaanite tribute they let their aristocracy decay, appointing neither a senate nor the other magistrates their laws required. For Josephus the cycle begins as a failure of government.

Rashi explains Timnath-heres (v. 9) as “image of the sun”: such an image was set over Joshua’s grave, as if to say, alas, the man who stopped the sun lies buried. On v. 15, where the hand of the LORD is against Israel wherever they go, he follows Seder Olam and names Elimelech and his two sons, whose deaths open the book of Ruth, a story set in the days of the judges (Ruth 1:1).
traditions.cite: Rashi on Judges 2:9, 15; Seder Olam Rabbah 12

traditions.text: In this retelling Deborah’s first speech puts v. 19 into a picture. While Moses, Joshua, Kenaz and Zebul lived, she tells the people, you seemed obedient, but when they died your heart died too. You are like iron thrust into the fire, which runs like water while it burns and goes back to its hardness when it comes out.

In his sermon at Antioch in Pisidia, Paul compresses this chapter into one line: after the land was divided, God gave Israel judges “about the space of four hundred and fifty years,” until Samuel the prophet. He tells it as a gift in a history that leads to David and to Jesus, not as a cycle of failure. His figure is one of several ancient attempts to total the book’s years.

Augustine asks why God is said to have “sold” Israel (v. 14) when no price was paid, for Psalm 44:12 has God selling his people for nought. His answer: the oppressors’ idolatry was a kind of price, since by not worshiping God they earned the people handed over to them. Israel, sold for nothing, would be redeemed “without money” (Isaiah 52:3), by the blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). On vv. 21–23 he adds that the nations were left to test Israel and would have vanished had Israel obeyed.

On v. 3 Augustine draws a hard conclusion: when God threatens that the nations’ gods will be a snare, some sins come about as an effect of divine anger, a punishment that consists in sinning. On v. 10 he explains how a generation could fail to know the LORD: they had not seen the wonders by which he had made himself known to their fathers.

3.overview:
Verses 1–6 finish the book’s introduction: the LORD left the Philistines, Canaanites, Sidonians and Hivites to test Israel and to teach war to a generation that had not known it, and Israel married their daughters and served their gods. Then come the first deliverers. Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, frees Israel from Chushan-rishathaim after eight years. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, brings Moab’s tribute to the very fat King Eglon, asks to see him alone, and stabs him in his cool upper room. The servants wait outside, thinking the king is relieving himself, while Ehud escapes and leads Israel to hold the Jordan fords. Shamgar kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.

Othniel’s story is the book’s pattern with almost nothing added; Ehud’s is the same pattern told at length. Side by side, they show how a bare formula becomes a story.

3.hermeneutics:
Tribute was delivered in person and in procession. On the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (about 825 BC), found at Nimrud, the delegations of five subject rulers file before the Assyrian king in carved panels. The Israelite one, labeled the tribute of Jehu, brings silver, gold, golden vessels and a staff for the king while its leader bows to the ground. Ehud’s “present” (vv. 15, 17, 18) is *minchah*, the same Hebrew word used when Moab pays tribute to David (2 Samuel 8:2) and Hoshea to Assyria (2 Kings 17:3). That makes Ehud a vassal’s envoy at an expected audience, the one Israelite with a reason to come near the king. He sends the bearers away (v. 18) and returns alone with a private word, a request a king might grant a loyal subject.

Shamgar is “the son of Anath” (v. 31), and Anat was the warrior goddess of Canaan, known from the Ugaritic myths for slaughtering her enemies in battle. Bronze arrowheads inscribed *ben-anat*, “son of Anat,” have been found from the 11th century BC and later, and several scholars take the phrase as a fighter’s title rather than a father’s name. His own name is not Hebrew; many now think it Hurrian. Read that way, the man who “also delivered Israel” bears a Canaanite war name, and v. 31 gives him no tribe, no oppression and no years of rest. The Song of Deborah remembers his days as a time when the highways were empty (5:6).

notes: **What each panel has:** Ehud’s fills D′ with the dagger, the private room and the locked doors. Othniel’s has the one thing Ehud’s lacks: “the Spirit of the LORD came upon him” (v. 10).

**Hand:** the Hebrew word for hand (*yad*) comes five times in vv. 15–30. Ehud is “bound in his right hand” (KJV “lefthanded”), Israel sends the tribute by his hand (v. 15), he puts forth his left hand (v. 21), and Moab is given into Israel’s hand (vv. 28, 30). He is a Benjamite, a “son of the right hand.”

**Word and blow:** the “secret errand” (v. 19) and the “message from God” (v. 20) are the same Hebrew word, *davar*. The verb for thrusting the dagger (v. 21) is the verb for blowing the trumpet (v. 27).

Verses 1–6 close the book’s second introduction (2:6–3:6) by naming the nations left to test Israel. Verse 7 opens the section of deliverers with the formula of 2:11, “did evil in the sight of the LORD,” and the first group follows: Othniel of Judah, Ehud of Benjamin, and Shamgar, whose tribe is not given, before the formula returns in 4:1.

**Backward and forward:** Othniel comes from 1:13 and Joshua 15:17, so the first judge is a man the conquest already knew. Ehud’s left-handed Benjamites return as the slingers of 20:16, and Shamgar is remembered in the Song of Deborah (5:6).

traditions.text: A thematic link. Like Ehud, the Nephite captain Teancum strikes at an invading king himself. He steals by night into Amalickiah’s tent and puts a javelin to his heart before the servants wake, and years later kills Amalickiah’s brother Ammoron the same way, though that time the servants wake and kill him. Both stories turn on a king alone and guards slow to learn what has happened.

Josephus makes Chushan “King of the Assyrians” and says that some Israelites were taken by siege and others submitted out of fear, paying a crushing tribute for eight years. Othniel acts on an admonition from God, finds a few helpers, destroys Chushan’s garrison first, and only then, as more join him, drives the Assyrians back over the Euphrates. The one verse of battle in v. 10 becomes a small revolt that grows.

The Talmud finds Laban behind Chushan-rishathaim. A baraita says Beor, Cushan-rishathaim and Laban the Aramean are one man, called *rishathaim*, “double wickedness,” because he did Israel evil twice: pursuing Jacob to kill him and oppressing Israel in the days of the judges. The link starts in the text, since Chushan is king of Aram-naharaim, the land of Laban’s family (Genesis 24:10).

The midrash hears “he judged Israel” (v. 10) as an argument with God. Othniel pleaded, it says, that God had promised Moses to deliver Israel whether or not they did his will, reading the doubled verb of “I have surely seen” in Exodus 3:7 as that promise. Rashi takes the verse the same way: Othniel’s judging was his plea before God, not a case in court.

This early chronicle counts the years of oppression inside each judge’s term rather than adding them: Othniel’s forty include Chushan’s eight, and Ehud’s eighty include Eglon’s eighteen. Shamgar it places at the end of Ehud’s days, inside the eighty years. It also sets Ruth’s family in Moab during Eglon’s reign, the king of vv. 12–30.

Pseudo-Philo has no Othniel and no Ehud; its first judge is Kenaz, whom Judges names as Othniel’s father. In its great battle Kenaz goes down alone at night, the spirit of the Lord “clothed him as a garment,” and the Amorites, struck blind, kill one another. Afterward his hand cleaves to the sword, as the hand of David’s warrior Eleazar did (2 Samuel 23:10). Its only Aod is a later Midianite sorcerer.

Josephus’s Ehud lives at Jericho and wins Eglon’s favor with presents. He strikes at midday in summer, when the guards are off watch because of the heat and gone to dinner. He tells the king he has a dream to impart by God’s command, and Eglon leaps from his throne for joy. Josephus adds that Shamgar, chosen next, died in the first year of his rule.

The Hebrew calls Ehud “bound” or “shut” in his right hand. The Targum, as Rashi reads it, takes this to mean his right arm was shrunken, so that he could use only his left. The Greek translators took the opposite view and made him a man who could use both hands alike, the skill 1 Chronicles 12:2 credits to Saul’s Benjamite kinsmen.

Eglon rises from his seat at the words “a message from God” (v. 20). The Talmud draws a rule from it: if a gentile king stood for God’s name in a mere title, a Jew must stand all the more for the divine name, and judges hearing it stand. Rashi adds that for rising, Eglon was rewarded with a descendant, Ruth, whom the Talmud calls Eglon’s granddaughter.
traditions.cite: b. Sanhedrin 60a; b. Nazir 23b; Rashi on Judges 3:20

traditions.text: Augustine asks whether Ehud lied when he spoke of a secret word and then a word of God. He thinks not. Scripture sometimes calls a deed a word, and that was the case here; and the word of God can be taken as God’s own order, since God had raised Ehud up as a savior and in those times such orders came from heaven.

Augustine’s Greek text says Shamgar killed six hundred men “besides the young oxen,” and he guesses that oxen died in the fight too. He notes that the version made from the Hebrew lacks those words and has the six hundred killed with a ploughshare. He also asks how Shamgar could save Israel when Israel was not enslaved, and answers that he kept an enemy from doing harm.

4.overview:
After Ehud’s death Israel again does evil, and the LORD sells them to Jabin, king of Canaan in Hazor, whose general Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots and oppresses Israel for twenty years. Deborah, a prophetess who judges Israel under a palm tree in the hills of Ephraim, summons Barak of Naphtali and gives him the LORD’s command to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor. Barak will go only if she goes, and she tells him the honor will then go to a woman. At the Kishon the LORD routs Sisera’s army. Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who gives him milk, covers him, and drives a tent peg through his temples while he sleeps.

Deborah’s words in v. 9 mislead on purpose. The woman who will take the honor seems to be Deborah herself, until Jael steps out of her tent in v. 18.

4.hermeneutics:
Sisera’s name has no clear Semitic meaning, and his base is Harosheth “of the Gentiles,” literally “of the nations” (v. 2). Proposals for the name run from Hurrian and Hittite to Egyptian and Philistine. The archaeologist Adam Zertal tied Sisera to the Sherden, one of the Sea Peoples, and placed Harosheth at el-Ahwat near the Wadi Ara; neither idea has won agreement. The setting does fit a north with newcomers in it. In the Egyptian *Story of Wenamun*, set about 1075 BC, the port of Dor is ruled by Beder, a prince of the Tjeker, another of the Sea Peoples. Read against that background, the enemy of ch. 4 may be an alliance: a Canaanite king in Hazor, and a general based among the mixed peoples of the plain with a lowland army of chariots.

Heber the Kenite (v. 11) belonged to a clan tied to Moses’ family that had come up with Judah (1:16) and then split off. Since the 19th century many scholars have linked the Kenites with metalwork, because their name is related to an Aramaic word for a smith and their southern country bordered the copper district of the Arabah. No ancient source calls them smiths, so the idea remains a hypothesis. It would explain v. 17, though: a clan of metalworkers living near a king with nine hundred chariots had good reason to keep the peace with Hazor. Jael kills him with what any tent dweller had at hand, a tent peg and a mallet.

structure.summary: Inclusio: Jabin “king of Canaan” and the “hand” open and close the chapter (vv. 2, 23–24).

open.text: The LORD sells Israel into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan

close.text: God subdues Jabin king of Canaan; Israel’s hand prevails

notes: **Sold into the hand:** the LORD “sold” Israel into Jabin’s hand (v. 2), and the verb returns when Deborah says he will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (v. 9). The Hebrew word for hand comes six times (vv. 2, 7, 9, 14, 21, 24); the last two are Jael’s hand on the hammer and Israel’s hand on Jabin.
**Going out:** the LORD has “gone out” before Barak (v. 14); Jael “went out” to meet Sisera (v. 18) and “came out” to meet Barak (v. 22). One Hebrew verb links the three.

**The tent:** v. 11 seems to interrupt, but it plants Heber’s tent near Kedesh. The Hebrew word for tent comes five times (vv. 11, 17, 18, 20, 21), and the commander of nine hundred chariots dies in one.

Chapters 4 and 5 tell one victory twice, first in prose and then in the Song of Deborah, and the unit closes with the formula of rest, “the land had rest forty years” (5:31). The prose gives the places and the order of events; the song adds the tribes who came and those who stayed home.

**Backward and forward:** Jabin of Hazor recalls the king Joshua killed there (Joshua 11:1, 10). The verb for the LORD’s rout of Sisera (v. 15, “discomfited”) is the one used of Pharaoh’s army at the sea (Exodus 14:24, “troubled”), and Samuel remembers Sisera as “captain of the host of Hazor” (1 Samuel 12:9).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to “before” in v. 14 points to the Lord’s promise to his elders: “I will go before your face,” with his angels round about them to bear them up. Deborah tells Barak the same thing in the form of a question, that the LORD has already gone out before him. The footnote also lists Ether 1:42, where the Lord promises to go before Jared’s people into a choice land.

For v. 2, where the LORD “sold” Israel to Jabin, the Church’s footnote points to Isaiah 50 as Jacob reads it in the Book of Mormon. The Lord asks to which of his creditors he has sold his people and answers, “for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves.” God is the seller in the formula of Judges, but the price was Israel’s own doing. The same picture of a sale returns each time the book’s formula is used, from Chushan (3:8) to the Philistines and Ammon (10:7).

Josephus gives Jabin 300,000 footmen, 10,000 horsemen and 3,000 chariots, and he translates the names: Deborah means a bee and Barak lightning. When Barak will not lead without her, Deborah answers with indignation that he is handing to a woman the authority God gave him. His Jael gives Sisera sour milk, of which he drinks so much that he falls asleep. Josephus also fills out v. 24: Barak met Jabin at Hazor, killed him, and razed the city to its foundations.

Pseudo-Philo makes Jael a deliberate actor. She adorns herself and goes out to meet Sisera, who sees roses scattered on her bed and promises to marry her. While he sleeps she milks the flock and asks God for a sign: if he wakes and asks for water, her prayer is heard. He does, she mixes wine with the milk, and before driving the stake she asks God to strengthen her arm, words the translator compares with Judith 13:7.

The Talmud counts Deborah among the seven prophetesses of Israel. It reads “wife of Lapidoth” as “woman of flames,” because she made wicks for the sanctuary. Why say she sat under a palm tree? Rabbi Shimon ben Avshalom answers that she judged in the open so as never to be alone indoors with a man; another view says that as a palm has one heart, Israel in her day had one heart toward God.

A few lines later the same tractate turns critical. Rav Nahman says pride does not suit a woman, and he names two proud prophetesses whose names are those of creatures, Deborah the hornet and Huldah the weasel. The proof for Deborah is v. 6: she “sent and called Barak” instead of going to him herself. Josephus took the same name kindly, as “a bee.”

The Targum reads v. 5 as a list of Deborah’s holdings, not her address. She lived in Ataroth, it says, and owned palms in Jericho, orchards in Ramah, olive groves near Bethel and white earth on the King’s Mountain. Rashi accepts this and concludes that she was a woman of independent means. On v. 19 he explains the milk: milk makes a man drowsy, so Jael gave it in place of water.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on Judges 4:5; Rashi on 4:5, 19

traditions.text: In the roll of the faithful, the writer runs out of time to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah. Barak, not Deborah or Jael, is the name taken from this chapter, among those who “turned to flight the armies of the aliens” (11:34). He is counted with the faithful although v. 9 gives the honor of the day to a woman.

The Greek adds a reason to Barak’s condition in v. 8: “I know not the day on which the Lord prospers his messenger” with me. Augustine asks why Barak could not simply learn the day from the prophetess. He also asks whether the words mean that even angels succeed only with the Lord’s help, or only that the Lord gives success through an angel.
traditions.cite: Judges 4:8 LXX (Brenton 1844); Questions on the Heptateuch 7.26

traditions.text: Augustine takes “the LORD discomfited Sisera” (v. 15) as an example of how scripture shows God acting on hearts: God terrifies and stuns Sisera in order to deliver him up. On v. 22, where Barak goes in to Jael, he warns that the expression, which often means sexual union, here means only that Barak entered her dwelling.

5.overview:
Deborah and Barak sing the victory of chapter 4. The LORD marches out of Seir and the earth shakes. Before Deborah arose, the roads were empty and the villages abandoned. Then the tribes are called by name: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali came, while Reuben stayed with his sheep, Gilead beyond Jordan, Dan with his ships and Asher by the sea. The kings of Canaan fight at Taanach, the stars fight from heaven, and the Kishon sweeps them away. Meroz is cursed. Jael is blessed, and Sisera falls dead at her feet.

The last scene belongs to the enemy. Sisera’s mother looks out of her window and asks why his chariot is so slow, and her wise ladies answer for her: he must be dividing the spoil, a girl or two for every man. The hearer already knows where he lies. The poem lets her hope stand unanswered, then closes with a single line of prayer.

5.hermeneutics:
Canaanite poets at Ugarit (13th century BC) built some lines in steps. A line starts, breaks off, and is repeated with something added, as in a couplet of the Baal cycle (KTU 1.2 IV 8–9) that calls out “your enemy, O Baal” twice before saying what Baal will do to him; Psalm 92:9 follows the same pattern. The Song of Deborah climbs this way again and again: “I, even I, will sing,” “awake, awake,” “the kings came and fought, then fought the kings of Canaan” (vv. 3, 12, 19). What reads in English as repetition is a form Israel’s earliest poets shared with Canaan, and it slows the song at the moments that matter.

“In Taanach by the waters of Megiddo” (v. 19) names two cities about five miles apart on the southwest edge of the Jezreel valley. W. F. Albright (1936) asked why a poet would place the battle by the lesser town and answered that Megiddo then lay in ruins, which would date the song to the later 12th century BC. Later study of Megiddo’s levels has made that gap less certain, and critics call his premise an assumption. The debate still shows how closely the song fits a real landscape.

Carved ivory plaques of the 9th–8th centuries BC, from Nimrud, Arslan Tash, Khorsabad and Samaria, show a woman’s face framed in a window above a balustrade. The “woman at the window” was a stock image of the Phoenician and Syrian courts, and the Bible gives the pose to royal women: Michal watching David (2 Samuel 6:16), Jezebel waiting for Jehu (2 Kings 9:30). Sisera’s mother takes it in v. 28, a lady of a Canaanite house, safe behind her lattice.

rows.text: Praise: the LORD’s march and Israel before Deborah

notes: **Two mothers:** the word “mother” comes only twice, for Deborah, “a mother in Israel” (v. 7), and for Sisera’s mother (v. 28). Jael stands between them.

**Blessing moves:** “bless” comes four times. The people bless the LORD (vv. 2, 9); then Jael is twice “blessed above women” (v. 24). The LORD is named 14 times, and none after v. 23 until the last prayer.
**The fall:** v. 27 says “bowed” three times and “fell” three times, slowing Sisera’s death to a frame-by-frame view.

Chapters 4–5 form one unit: the victory told in prose, then sung, as Exodus 14 is followed by the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15. The closing formula, “the land had rest forty years” (v. 31), ends the Deborah story the way 3:11 and 3:30 end Othniel’s and Ehud’s, and 6:1 starts the next round of the cycle.

**Echoes:** Psalm 68:7–8 opens with the same march, the earth shaking and the heavens dropping “even Sinai itself.” Psalm 83:9–10 prays for Israel’s enemies to fall like Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon.

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 5, where the mountains melt before the LORD, sends the reader to Restoration texts with the same image. In the Kirtland Temple dedicatory prayer the Saints ask the Lord to “cause the mountains to flow down at thy presence” (D&C 109:74), and D&C 133:40 has the Saints of the last days pray for the same. In Moses 6:34 the Lord promises Enoch that the mountains shall flee before him. The theophany of the song becomes a pattern for God’s coming again.

This Jewish retelling of biblical history gives Deborah a new hymn. It begins with Abraham, the binding of Isaac and Sinai, then calls the sun, moon and stars God’s witnesses and says that in Sisera’s day God ordered the stars out of their ranks to burn his enemies. It names Sisera’s mother Themech and has her plan to meet her son with the Hebrew women he will bring home. Deborah ends at Shiloh, sounding the trumpets as a testimony “between the stars and the Lord of them.”

Josephus passes over the song entirely but takes its weather into his account. A great storm of rain and hail came down in the battle, and the wind drove it into the Canaanites’ faces so that their arrows and slings were useless, while it struck the Israelites from behind. Some of the enemy fell by their own horses and chariots, close to the song’s broken horsehoofs (v. 22).

The book of Judith tells of a widow who kills an enemy general in his tent, and it borrows Jael’s blessing for her. When she returns with Holofernes’ head, the elder Ozias says she is blessed of God “above all the women upon the earth.” The words echo v. 24, and Pseudo-Philo in turn has Jael boast that she killed Sisera with her own hands, wording that recalls Judith.

Rav taught that a prophet who becomes proud loses prophecy, and his proof is Deborah. She sang “until that I Deborah arose” (v. 7), praising herself, so her prophetic spirit left her, and the song has to call her back: “Awake, awake, Deborah” (v. 12). Rashi repeats this on v. 12 but first gives the plain sense, a call to sing more strongly.

The rabbis built their rules for banning an offender out of v. 23, “Curse ye Meroz.” Each phrase supplies a step: the curse is announced by the angel, a messenger of authority; it is doubled for one who will not mend; it reaches all who live with him; and it states his offense, that they came not to help the LORD. Ulla says Barak banned Meroz with four hundred trumpet blasts. Some sages say Meroz was a great man, others a star that would not join the stars of v. 20.

The “women in the tent” above whom Jael is blessed (v. 24) are Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, each tied to a tent in Genesis. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak uses the verse to argue that a transgression done for the sake of Heaven equals a commandment kept for the wrong reason. Rabbi Yohanan reads the repeated “bowed, fell, lay” of v. 27 as Sisera forcing himself on Jael before he died; the rabbis count her act as done for Heaven’s sake.

The Torah calls the New Year “a day of blowing the trumpets” (Numbers 29:1), and the Aramaic Targum renders it a day of *yevava*. To learn what that sound is, the rabbis turn to v. 28, where Sisera’s mother “cried” (*vateyabev*) through the lattice. One view hears broken sighs, the other short whimpers, and the two become the patterns of the shofar blasts still sounded on Rosh Hashanah.

Why is the Kishon “that ancient river” (v. 21)? A tale in the Talmud says that at the Red Sea the sea gave up Pharaoh’s drowned army only when the Kishon stood surety to repay it. When the stars fell on Sisera’s men, their iron spears grew hot, they went down to cool them in the Kishon, and the river swept them into the sea, paying the old debt. Rashi cites the story on v. 21.

Ambrose holds up Deborah, whom he takes for a widow, as proof that “it is not sex, but valour which makes strong,” and he makes Barak her son. In Jael he sees the Church of the Gentiles winning the victory the Jewish army began. Sisera’s thirst quenched with milk (v. 25) means the enemy overcome by wisdom, since what feeds the faithful weakens their foe.

Augustine’s Latin Bible, following the Greek, read v. 8 as “they chose new gods like barley bread.” He untangles the word order so the line runs: the people failed and chose new gods until Deborah arose, and then they took the princes’ cities. He then asks how false gods can be likened to bread that feeds, and answers that the likeness is in the eyes of those who chose, who thought a cheap food would still give life.

When Mary visits Elizabeth, Elizabeth greets her with “Blessed art thou among women.” Many readers since the early church have heard in it the blessing of Jael “above women” (v. 24) and of Judith, the two Israelite women blessed for crushing an enemy’s head. Luke turns the phrase to a woman blessed for the child she carries.

6.overview:
For seven years Midian, Amalek and the people of the east swarm in at harvest with their tents and camels, stripping the land. Israel hides in caves and cries out. A prophet answers first: God brought them out of Egypt, and they have not obeyed. Then the angel of the LORD comes to Ophrah, where Gideon is beating out wheat in a winepress, and sends him to save Israel. Gideon asks for a sign; fire springs from the rock and eats his offering. That night he pulls down his father’s altar to Baal. When Midian camps in Jezreel, the Spirit comes on him, the clans rally, and he tests God twice with a fleece.

Gideon’s first fight is at home. Before he faces Midian he must break his own father’s altar, and he does it by night because he is afraid. The town wants him dead, and his father’s retort gives him his second name.

6.hermeneutics:
The oldest Assyrian record of camels in war is the Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III, which lists among the coalition he fought at Qarqar in 853 BC “1,000 camels of Gindibu the Arab.” Camel riders could cross the desert, strike and withdraw beyond reach. Judges 6 is the Bible’s first picture of such raiders: Midianites, Amalekites and the “children of the east” come with their tents and herds “as grasshoppers,” their camels “without number” (v. 5), and range as far as Gaza (v. 4). The threat is not an army to be met in the field but a yearly swarm at harvest, and Israel answers by hiding food in caves and dens (v. 2).

Grain was threshed on an open floor on high ground, where the wind could carry off the chaff. A winepress was a vat cut into the rock among the vines, low and out of sight. Both are common finds in the Iron Age hill country. Gideon beating out wheat in a winepress (v. 11) is a man working in a pit to stay hidden, and that is where the angel calls him a “mighty man of valour.”

In 2019 excavators at Khirbet al-Ra‘i, near Lachish, found a jug of about 1100 BC with five letters in ink in the early alphabet, read as *yrb‘l*, Jerubbaal (Rollston and others, 2021). It is the first time the name has turned up outside the Bible. The excavators allow that it may belong to another man, since the site lies far south of Ophrah. It does show that a name built on Baal was in ordinary use in this period. Verse 32 explains Gideon’s second name as a taunt, “Let Baal plead,” and the book keeps calling him by it (7:1; 8:29, 35).

rows.text: Oppression, the cry, the prophet’s rebuke
The call and the first sign

notes: **Who saves?** The verb “save” comes five times. The LORD sends Gideon to save Israel (v. 14); Gideon asks how he can (v. 15); Joash asks the townsmen whether they will save Baal (v. 31); and Gideon twice asks God to save Israel by his hand (vv. 36–37).
**Plead:** Joash’s retort uses the verb “plead” or “contend” four times in vv. 31–32, and the name Jerubbaal is built on it.
**The fleece:** the word comes seven times in vv. 37–40, and “altar” eight times in vv. 24–32.

Chapter 6 opens the Gideon unit (6:1–8:35) with the book’s formula: Israel did evil, and the LORD gave them into an enemy’s hand (cf. 3:7–8; 4:1–2). This time a prophet rebukes them before any deliverer comes (vv. 7–10). The story runs three chapters, longer than any judge’s but Samson’s, and Paul Tanner (1992), building on D. W. Gooding, reads it as the center of the book’s symmetrical design.
**Echoes:** the angel who accepts an offering on a rock and vanishes in fire returns at Samson’s birth, where he ascends in the flame (13:19–20).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to Gideon’s question about the miracles “which our fathers told us of” (v. 13) points to Moroni’s answer to the same complaint. God has not ceased to be a God of miracles, Moroni writes; miracles stop when people dwindle in unbelief and depart from the right way. The prophet of vv. 8–10 gives Gideon much the same answer before the angel arrives: Israel has not obeyed.

A thematic link. In D&C 63 the Lord says that “faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe,” and that he is not pleased with those who seek signs “for faith.” Korihor demands a sign before he will believe and is given one to his ruin. Judges does not condemn Gideon, who already believes and asks to know he is not mistaken; God grants each test without rebuke, and the contrast with Korihor turns on that difference.

Josephus adds that the Midianites let Israel plough in winter so that there would be a crop to carry off in summer. The visitor at the winepress appears “in the shape of a young man,” and when he calls Gideon a happy man beloved of God, Gideon answers with a wry joke: a fine sign of God’s favor, that he must use a winepress for a threshing floor. Josephus says nothing of the altar of Baal or the fleece.

Here the angel tells Gideon that Israel’s troubles are its own doing, and that God will rescue them for the sake of the fathers who sleep. Gideon justifies his request for a sign by pointing out that Moses, “the first of all the prophets,” asked for one too. The angel has him pour water on the rock and choose what it will become; he asks for half blood and half fire, and the two burn together without quenching or consuming each other.

Rashi, following the midrash, dates the call to Passover. Gideon’s complaint about the miracles of the fathers (v. 13) means: last night my father read the Hallel, and I heard the psalm of Israel going out of Egypt, yet now God has left us. The unleavened cakes of v. 19 confirm the season, and the barley loaf of the next chapter points to the barley offering of that week. “Go in this thy might” (v. 14) means the merit Gideon earned by pleading Israel’s case.

Gideon’s offering broke almost every rule of sacrifice, and the rabbis counted the exceptions. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana lists eight things permitted that one night: sacrifice away from the tabernacle, at night, by a man who was not a priest, without sacred vessels, with wood and vessels from the Asherah, and with a bull set apart for idolatry and perhaps worshipped. Rashi repeats the list on v. 26. Augustine asked the same question (below).

Rashi notices that the first sign only half works. The fleece is soaked, “a bowl full of water,” but the ground around it is not dry, because God’s covenant promises that dew always falls. That is why Gideon asks for the test the other way round, a dry fleece on wet ground, which no one could explain away.

Ambrose opens his treatise on the Holy Spirit with Gideon. The dew on the fleece is the faith once given to Israel, and the dew on the whole ground is the Spirit poured out on the Gentiles, as the Psalm says in its Greek and Latin form, where the Lord comes down like rain upon a fleece (Psalm 72:6). Asked whether Gideon lacked faith in asking for more signs, he answers that Gideon spoke in mysteries: “He was not then doubtful, but careful that we should not doubt.”

Augustine is less sure than his teacher Ambrose. He wonders whether Gideon broke the command not to tempt the LORD (Deuteronomy 6:16), since Gideon himself asks God not to be angry (v. 39). Yet he reads the fleece the same way: wet first like Israel, then dry while the Church receives the dew. God, he concludes, used a faith that faltered both to save his people and to foretell what he would do.

On v. 12 he notes that the Latin should read “The Lord is with thee, mighty in strength,” with the might belonging to God, not to Gideon. He asks how Gideon could sacrifice away from the tabernacle at Shiloh and answers that God, who gave the law to men, could command an exception through his angel, as with Abraham and Elijah. The fire from the rock, like the water from the rock in the desert, stands for the gift of the Spirit.

7.overview:
Gideon camps at the spring of Harod with thirty-two thousand men, and the LORD says they are too many. The fearful are sent home, and ten thousand remain. At the water the LORD has Gideon set apart those who lap; three hundred do, and with them alone he will save Israel. That night Gideon creeps down to the enemy camp and hears a Midianite tell a dream of a barley loaf flattening a tent, which his comrade reads as the sword of Gideon. Gideon worships, arms his men with trumpets and lamps hidden in jars, and at his signal they blow, smash the jars and shout. Midian turns its swords on itself and flees, and Ephraim seizes the fords and kills the princes Oreb and Zeeb.

The reason for the shrinking army is given in v. 2: so that Israel cannot boast, “Mine own hand hath saved me.” Everything after is built to make that boast impossible.

7.hermeneutics:
At Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC), officials sent their king dreams that bore on war. In one letter (ARM 26 233) the governor Itur-Asdu reports that a man named Malik-Dagan dreamed he went into Dagan’s temple at Terqa, where the god promised to make the Yaminite kings flounder in a fisherman’s chest and set them before King Zimri-Lim. Itur-Asdu writes it down, sends it on, and asks the king to check it. Dreams like this were treated as intelligence, and they promised the dreamer’s own side victory. In v. 13 the dream comes to a soldier in the enemy camp, and his comrade reads it at once as Midian’s defeat. Gideon gets his assurance from Midian’s own sleep, and he worships before he fights (v. 15).

Babylonian texts divide the night into three watches: evening, middle and morning. Israel reckoned the same way, with a “morning watch” (Exodus 14:24) and the “beginning of the watches” at nightfall (Lamentations 2:19). Gideon strikes at “the beginning of the middle watch,” when the new guards “had but newly set the watch” (v. 19). The sentries just relieved are going to sleep and the new ones are not yet alert, so three hundred men with noise and sudden light can make a sleeping camp believe it is surrounded by an army. Josephus, who wrote in a Roman world of four watches, moved the attack to the fourth (see Traditions).

notes: **Hand:** the word comes 13 times. Israel must not say “mine own hand” saved it (v. 2); instead the LORD gives Midian “into thine hand” (vv. 7, 9, 14, 15), and the men’s hands hold only trumpets, jars and lamps (vv. 16, 20).
**Camp:** “host” or “camp” comes 17 times, mostly of Midian’s vast camp, against “three hundred,” named five times (vv. 6, 7, 8, 16, 22).
**Trumpet:** the ram’s horn sounds eight times. The only swords drawn are Midian’s, turned on one another (v. 22).

The chapter is the heart of the Gideon unit (6:1–8:35). Paul Tanner (1992) reads 6:33–7:18 as its center, the stretch where a fearful Gideon is brought to confidence, and the turn comes when he worships after hearing the dream (v. 15). The story runs straight on into ch. 8, where Gideon crosses the Jordan after the kings.

**Echoes:** sending home the fearful follows the law of war in Deuteronomy 20:8. Jonathan later says nothing restrains the LORD “to save by many or by few” (1 Samuel 14:6), and at Michmash too a panicked camp turns its swords on itself (1 Samuel 14:20).

traditions.text: Nephi copies Isaiah 9–10 from the brass plates, and both chapters remember this battle. In 2 Nephi 20:26 the Lord will scourge Assyria “according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb,” the rock of v. 25. In 2 Nephi 19:4, the parallel to Isaiah 9:4, the yoke is broken, but the closing phrase of the KJV, the day of Midian, does not appear.

The Church’s footnote to v. 4, where the LORD will try the people at the water, glosses “try” as “test” and points to two passages that use the word. In D&C 98:12 the Lord says he will give the faithful line upon line and “try you and prove you herewith.” In Alma 27:15 Ammon goes ahead to try the hearts of the Nephites before the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi follow.

A thematic link to v. 2. Mormon writes that the Nephites who boasted “in their own strength” were left in their own strength and driven before the Lamanites. The Lord’s preface to the Doctrine and Covenants says the weak things of the world will break down the mighty, so that man should not trust in the arm of flesh.

Josephus reverses the test. God has Gideon bring the army to the river at noon, in the heat, and count as brave those who kneel to drink and as fearful those who drink “hastily and tumultuously.” The three hundred chosen are the fearful ones, so that no one can credit the victory to courage. In his version God tells Gideon this in his sleep.

The dreamer’s comrade explains the barley loaf: barley is the poorest seed, and the Israelites are known as the poorest people of Asia, so the loaf is Gideon’s army. The attack comes in the fourth watch, and the cry is “Victory to Gideon, by God’s assistance.” Most of the Midianites die at their allies’ hands, Josephus says, because the camp held nations of many languages who took one another for enemies in the dark.

Pseudo-Philo leaves out the shrinking army and the dream. Gideon goes straight to the edge of the camp and overhears the Midianites saying that the sword of Gideon is coming, that their sins are full, and that their own gods had warned them and they did not believe. Clothed with the spirit of the Lord, Gideon leads the three hundred down, and they cry, “The sword of the Lord is upon us.”

Rashi reads vv. 5–6 as one test, not two. Those who knelt and bent down to lap the water with their faces were sent away because they were used to kneeling before idols; the three hundred brought the water up by hand and did not bow at all. The trumpets and torches of v. 16 recall Sinai, where the shofar sounded and fire came down, and in the plain sense the torches lit a dark night and the jars hid them.

The rabbis ask why the dreamer sees barley. The loaf stands for the omer, the sheaf of barley offered at Passover, and in its merit Israel was saved in Gideon’s day; Rashi joins this to his dating of the call to Passover (6:19). They read the rare word for the loaf as a sign that the generation had been “emptied” of righteous men, so only the merit of the offering was left to save it.

Augustine follows the Greek text, which says the three hundred lapped “with their hand” and tongue: they threw water into their mouths and caught it like dogs. Three hundred in Greek numerals is the letter T, the shape of the cross, and a dog was a byword for something despised, so God won with what the world holds in contempt (1 Corinthians 1:27). Ambrose had already read the three hundred as a sign that the world would be freed “by the mystery of the cross.”
traditions.cite: Quaestiones in Heptateuchum 7.37; Ambrose, On the Holy Spirit 1, prologue 5

traditions.text: The barley loaf, he writes, means the same as the dogs: the Savior would confound the proud through the contemptible things of the world. On the battle cry he notes that the sword was to do what pleased both the Lord and Gideon, so the cry joins the two without making them equals.

No command from God is recorded for the jars and lamps, but Augustine is sure God inspired them. They foretell the apostles, who carry the light of the gospel “in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). When the martyrs’ bodies were broken like the jars, the light within shone out and overcame the enemies of the gospel.

8.overview:
Gideon calms Ephraim’s anger with praise, then crosses the Jordan after the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna. The towns of Succoth and Penuel refuse his tired men bread, and he promises to punish them. He takes the kings at Karkor, then tears Succoth’s elders with thorns and pulls down Penuel’s tower. He kills the kings himself for his brothers they slew at Tabor. Israel asks him to rule as a dynasty, and he refuses: “the LORD shall rule over you.” From the spoil he makes a gold ephod, and all Israel goes after it.

Gideon turns down the crown in words but takes much of what a king has: the royal spoil, a shrine in his own town, many wives, seventy sons, and a son by a concubine whom he names Abimelech, “my father is king.” Chapter 9 shows what that son makes of the name.

8.hermeneutics:
In v. 14 a young man of Succoth, caught on the road, “described” the town’s seventy-seven officials and elders; the Hebrew verb means he wrote them down. Alphabetic writing was spreading in the villages of this age. At Izbet Sartah, a small hill-country settlement near Aphek, excavators found a potsherd from about the 12th century BC with the alphabet scratched on it in order, most likely a learner’s practice piece. The verse takes for granted that a youth picked up at random could write out a list of names on the spot, and Gideon uses the list to find the men who mocked him.

Babylonian temple records describe the garments of divine statues, sewn with small gold ornaments and renewed for festivals, a subject A. L. Oppenheim gathered in “The Golden Garments of the Gods” (1949). Israel’s ephod was a priest’s vestment worked with gold (Exodus 28:6) and an object used to ask God’s will (1 Samuel 23:9). Gideon’s seventeen hundred shekels, about 19 kilograms of gold, besides purple and ornaments taken from the kings, would make something far heavier than a garment. Many scholars therefore picture a gold-covered cult object, perhaps the dress of an image, set up in Ophrah where people came to consult it. In a world where gods wore gold, a gold ephod in a leader’s hometown would draw worship, and v. 27 says it did.

notes: **The taunt returns:** Succoth’s question about the kings’ hands and the bread (v. 6) is quoted back word for word when Gideon brings the kings (v. 15). “Bread” comes only in those verses and v. 5.
**Two kings:** Zebah and Zalmunna are named 11 times, always as a pair, from v. 5 to their death in v. 21.
**Rule:** the verb comes four times in vv. 22–23, once in the people’s offer and three times in Gideon’s refusal, the last with the LORD as subject.

The chapter closes the Gideon unit (6:1–8:35) with the book’s formula, “the country was in quietness forty years” (v. 28), and then the pattern of 2:19: once the judge was dead, Israel turned back to the Baals. Tanner (1992) starts the Abimelech story at v. 33, since Baal-berith, the seventy sons and the Shechem concubine all return in 9:1–6.
**Echoes:** Gideon’s answer, “the LORD shall rule over you,” stands behind 1 Samuel 8:7, where the LORD says Israel’s demand for a king rejects him as their ruler.

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to the LORD who “shall rule over you” (v. 23) points to two Restoration texts. Mormon laments that people do not want the Lord their God, who created them, to rule and reign over them, though he is good and merciful to them, and that they will not have him as their guide. In D&C 60:4 the Lord declares that he rules in the heavens above and among the armies of the earth.

A thematic parallel to vv. 22–27. Alma’s people want him as king, and he refuses, telling them to trust no man to be a king over them. He gives his own past as a warning: under King Noah, he says, “I myself was caught in a snare,” and he was rescued only through repentance. Gideon refuses the same office, and the ephod he makes becomes a snare to him and to his house (v. 27).

A thematic parallel. When the Jaredites ask their leaders to anoint one of their sons king, the request grieves them, and the brother of Jared warns, “Surely this thing leadeth into captivity.” Jared lets the people choose, and the brother of Jared’s firstborn, Pagag, refuses the crown, as do all his brothers and all but one of Jared’s sons, much as Gideon refuses for himself and his son (v. 23). Ether’s record goes on to show the warning coming true, and Abimelech’s reign (ch. 9) follows a similar arc.

Josephus praises Gideon as a man of temper for turning away Ephraim’s anger, and says that by stopping a civil war he did Israel more good than by his victory. He leaves out Succoth and Penuel, the offer of a dynasty and the ephod. In their place, Gideon “would have laid down the government” but was persuaded to keep it, and judged Israel for forty years. Josephus kills the two kings at Ophrah, not in the field.

Pseudo-Philo is blunter than Judges. Gideon asks for the people’s gold armlets, and from twelve talents of gold he “made idols and worshipped them.” God explains why he does not punish him at once: Gideon had pulled down Baal’s sanctuary, and if he were struck now, people would say Baal had taken revenge. So Gideon dies in a good old age, and God will punish him after his death.

Rashi takes the gentler view of the ephod. Gideon made it as a memorial of the great deliverance, to show how vast the enemy had been, since even their earrings held so much gold; Israel went astray after it only after his death, and his own intention was pure. On v. 2 he explains the gleaning that beats the vintage: Ephraim’s capture of the two princes at the end outweighed Gideon’s first battle. On v. 5 he notes that the men of Succoth who refused were Israelites, not Canaanites.

Samuel’s list of deliverers puts Jerubbaal beside Moses and Samuel (1 Samuel 12:11). The rabbis draw a rule: Jerubbaal in his generation is like Moses in his, Bedan like Aaron, Jephthah like Samuel. Even the least distinguished man, once appointed over the community, must be obeyed like the greatest of the great. The point suits Gideon, who called himself the least in his father’s house (6:15).

Hebrews names “Gedeon” first among the judges who through faith turned to flight the armies of the aliens. Augustine asks how he can stand there after the ephod, which Scripture plainly condemns. His answer: Scripture praises the faith it finds and still records the sins it knows, and Gideon is commended for the good and faithful life in which he died.

How could a vestment be made from seventeen hundred shekels of gold? Augustine notes that Gideon “set it up,” as if it stood by itself, and suggests that the ephod may stand for a whole shrine furnished like the tabernacle. Gideon’s sin, he argues, was not making an idol of a false god but copying the tabernacle away from the place God had chosen, which became a kind of idol.

Augustine also asks how the land could rest forty years when Israel went whoring after the ephod. He answers that the writer told the gold’s story all at once, and the ephod belongs to the end of Gideon’s days. The worship of Baal-berith after his death, with no pretense of the fathers’ religion, was the greater sin and was not left unpunished.

9.overview:
Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine in Shechem, asks his mother's kin whether one ruler is better than seventy. With silver from the temple of Baal-berith he hires reckless men, kills his seventy brothers on one stone at Ophrah, and is made king. Only Jotham escapes. From Mount Gerizim he tells a fable: the trees offer kingship to the olive, fig and vine, who refuse, then to the bramble, who accepts. Three years later Shechem turns on Abimelech. He razes the city, burns about a thousand people in its stronghold, then dies at Thebez when a woman drops a millstone on him.

Watch the fire. Jotham asks that fire come out from Abimelech to devour Shechem, and from Shechem to devour Abimelech (v. 20). Both come true. Abimelech burns the stronghold of Shechem's tower (v. 49) and is struck down as he goes to burn the tower of Thebez (v. 52). The last words name it: “the curse of Jotham.”

9.hermeneutics:
Babylonian scribes liked debates between plants. In *Tamarisk and Palm*, copied from the 18th century BC and still read in Late Bronze Age Syria at Emar, a king plants both trees in his courtyard and they quarrel over which is worth more. The tamarisk boasts that its wood is carved into statues of the gods and that the king eats from its table; the palm answers that its fruit is served to royalty. Each tree claims the higher rank by listing whom it serves. Jotham turns the contest around. His olive, fig and vine also name their service, oil that honors “God and man” and wine that cheers them, and that is why they refuse to rule. Only the bramble, which gives nothing, wants the crown.

Shechem had bred a hill-country strongman before. In the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC, Lab'ayu of Shechem raids his neighbors, presses Megiddo and Gezer, and is accused of using Habiru fighters, landless men for hire. Answering Pharaoh, he defends himself with a proverb: an ant that is struck bites the hand that struck it (EA 252). He was finally killed, and his sons kept up the raids (EA 250). Abimelech repeats the pattern: a ruler based at Shechem, paid soldiers, war on nearby towns, a violent end.

The “piece of a millstone” (v. 53) is the upper stone of a household hand mill, a loaf-shaped stone pushed back and forth over a flat lower stone to grind grain each day. Grinding was women's work (Exodus 11:5; Matthew 24:41). The woman of Thebez brings the king down with a kitchen tool, the shame Abimelech tries to escape by having his armor-bearer finish him (v. 54).

notes: **Seventy:** the number comes 6 times, five for the murdered sons (vv. 2, 5, 18, 24, 56) and once for the silver that paid for them (v. 4).
**One:** Abimelech asks whether “one” should rule (v. 2), kills his brothers on “one stone” (vv. 5, 18), and dies by one woman (v. 53, KJV “a certain woman”).
**Lords of Shechem:** the Hebrew calls the townsmen *ba'ale*, “lords” or “owners,” 16 times, the same word as the god Baal-berith whose temple funds the murders.
**Fire and evil:** fire comes 5 times (vv. 15, 20 twice, 49, 52). God sends an “evil spirit” (v. 23) and at the end returns the evil on its doers (vv. 56–57).

Chapter 9 is the sequel to Gideon and stands as its own unit. It picks up two threads from 8:29–35: the son born to Gideon's concubine in Shechem (8:31) and Israel's turn to Baal-berith (8:33). Gideon refused a crown, saying the LORD would rule (8:23); his son seizes one, and Israel's first king is a failure. Tola then rises “after Abimelech” (10:1).
**Backward:** Gaal's call to “serve the men of Hamor” (v. 28) recalls Shechem's old ruling family in Genesis 34, and Joshua had renewed the covenant at Shechem a generation earlier (Joshua 24:1, 25).

traditions.text: A thematic link. King Mosiah warns the Nephites that “ye cannot dethrone an iniquitous king save it be through much contention,” with much bloodshed, because such a king has friends in iniquity and keeps guards about him. Abimelech's reign plays out the warning step by step: hired men put him on the throne, his brothers' blood pays for it, and he falls only after a revolt, two massacres and a siege.

Josephus sets Jotham's speech at a public festival in Shechem and lists the trees as fig, vine and then olive. He adds that the brier is “a sort of wood good for firing,” which explains its threat of fire, and has Jotham say his fable is no laughing matter. In his account the Shechemites repent of the murders and drive Abimelech out, and about fifteen hundred die in the burning stronghold, where Judges gives about a thousand (v. 49).

This retelling puts an apple tree where Judges has the olive, and each tree's refusal carries a prediction, ending “Abimelech shall die by stones.” The bramble makes a speech of its own: when Adam was condemned the earth brought forth thorns, and truth shone on Moses from a thorn bush, so truth will now be heard through the bramble. Here Abimelech rules a year and six months instead of three years and dies under half a millstone thrown from a tower.

The rabbis stop at the vine's words about wine “which cheereth God and man” (v. 13). If wine cheers people, how does it cheer God? Their answer is that the Levites sang in the temple only while the wine offering was poured on the altar, so this verse becomes the scriptural source for song at the libation. Rashi repeats the explanation in his comment on the verse.

Takes the same verse in another direction. Noah, it says, found a vine that had come out of the garden of Eden with its clusters still on it, ate of the fruit and rejoiced in his heart, and the proof text is the vine's boast here. He planted it, it ripened the same day, and he drank and was uncovered in his tent (Genesis 9:21).

Tanhuma sets this Abimelech against Abimelech of Gerar, who honored Abraham. Gideon's son killed his brothers on one stone, and since whoever digs a pit falls into it (Ecclesiastes 10:8), a stone killed him. God also shortened his years, as Proverbs 10:27 says of the wicked, which is why he ruled only three. Aggadat Bereshit puts him in a line with Cain, who killed Abel with a stone and died by one.

Uses the end of the chapter as an argument from the lesser to the greater. A woman on a tower, the weakest of the weak, brought down the mightiest man below with an upper millstone (v. 53). If a weak hand above can do that, the midrash asks, how much more can the God of heaven overcome the strong of the earth.

The Aramaic Targum softens v. 13: the vine's wine is poured as a libation before the LORD, and great men rejoice in it. Radak (David Kimhi) explains that the Targum keeps joy away from God, who has neither joy nor sorrow, since Scripture speaks in human language. He also reports his father's view that the three good trees answer the three generations Israel had offered Gideon, “thou, and thy son, and thy son's son” (8:22).
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on Judges 9:13; Radak on Judges 9:13

traditions.text: Following the midrash collection Yalkut Shimoni, Rashi reads the fable as a roll call of earlier judges. The olive is Othniel of Judah, the tribe Jeremiah 11:16 calls a green olive tree; the fig is Deborah; and the vine is Gideon, of Joseph's tribe, whom Genesis 49:22 likens to a fruitful bough. On Gaal's taunt (v. 28) he explains “the men of Hamor” as the family that ruled Shechem in Jacob's day (Genesis 34).

Augustine asks whether God sent the evil spirit of v. 23 by command or by permission, and admits it is not easy to decide. His Greek Bible's verb lets him read it as God releasing a spirit already eager to go, giving it power to break the peace between Abimelech and Shechem as a just punishment. On v. 15 he notes that the bramble's threat is a wish, let fire come out, which makes it sharper than a forecast.

Augustine argues that a story can signify truth without having happened, as with Aesop's fables, which no one is so untaught as to call lies. His example from Scripture is this chapter, where the trees seek a king and speak to the olive, the fig, the vine and the bramble. The narrative is invented, he says, “yet not a lying one,” because it points to something true. He uses it to answer heretics who claimed that Scripture permits lying.

10.overview:
Two quiet judgeships follow Abimelech: Tola of Issachar for twenty-three years at Shamir in Ephraim, and Jair of Gilead for twenty-two, with thirty sons who ride thirty donkeys and hold thirty towns. Then Israel serves the gods of every neighbor, and the LORD sells them to the Philistines and the Ammonites. For eighteen years Ammon crushes Gilead. When Israel cries out, the LORD recalls how often he has saved them and refuses to do it again: let the gods they chose save them. Israel confesses, puts away the foreign gods and serves the LORD. At the end Ammon is camped in Gilead, and Gilead's leaders want someone to lead.

Notice that the LORD never says yes. After his refusal the text says only that “his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel” (v. 16), in Hebrew that his soul grew short, the idiom for patience running out. No deliverer is raised up; in the next chapter Gilead hires one.

10.hermeneutics:
When Ur fell to the Elamites around 2000 BC, Sumerian poets mourned it in the *Lament for Ur*. The city's goddess Ningal tells how she wept before the great gods An and Enlil and begged them not to destroy her city or let its people perish. They would not hear: An is not one to change his command, the poem says, and Enlil does not alter what he has spoken. In that world a city's own patron pleaded with higher gods who would not move. In vv. 13–14 the LORD takes the hard line himself, “I will deliver you no more,” and then, with no intercessor named, he is the one who cannot bear Israel's misery (v. 16).

The gods in v. 6 were the real patrons of Israel's neighbors. Kings of Sidon, in inscriptions such as the sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II (5th century BC), record building temples for Baal of Sidon and for Astarte. Moab's god was Chemosh and Ammon's was Milcom (1 Kings 11:5, 7). The Philistines served Dagon (16:23), an old god of Syria known as Dagan in texts from Mari and with a temple at Ugarit. Each people expected its god to fight for it. Israel serves all of them, including the gods of the two nations now oppressing it (v. 7), and none of them helps. The LORD's taunt assumes the same logic: “go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen” (v. 14).

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, two brief judgeships and then the book's cycle told at its fullest.
notes: **Serve:** the verb comes 5 times (vv. 6 twice, 10, 13, 16). Israel “served not him” (v. 6); at the end it “served the LORD” (v. 16).
**Save:** Tola rises “to save” Israel (v. 1, KJV “defend”); the LORD recalls that he saved them (v. 12), refuses to save them again (v. 13), and tells their gods to do it (v. 14).
**Cry:** Israel cries (v. 10), is reminded that it cried before (v. 12), and is sent to cry to its gods (v. 14).
**A broken sentence:** in Hebrew v. 11 has no verb. The list of nations runs on into v. 12, and the KJV supplies “deliver.”

Chapter 10 opens the Jephthah section (10:1–12:15), which minor judges frame on both sides: Tola and Jair before Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon and Abdon after him. Verses 6–16 restate the cycle of 2:11–19 at greater length than anywhere else in the book, and vv. 17–18 set up chapter 11: Gilead needs a “head,” and Jephthah will bargain to become one (11:8–11).
**Forward:** v. 7 names two oppressors at once. Ammon is dealt with in chapters 11–12; the Philistines return in 13:1 for the Samson story.

traditions.text: A thematic link. Abinadi warns King Noah's people that unless they repent, the Lord will be slow to hear their cries and will let their enemies smite them. Under Lamanite bondage it happens: the Lord is slow to hear because of their iniquities, “nevertheless the Lord did hear their cries,” and he softens their oppressors' hearts before he frees them. The order matches vv. 10–16, a cry first refused and then heard, though in Mosiah the full deliverance still waits.

A thematic link, given to Saints driven from Jackson County. Because they were slow to hearken, the Lord is slow to answer their prayers in the day of their trouble; in peace they took his counsel lightly, but in trouble “of necessity they feel after me.” He adds that his bowels are filled with compassion and he will not utterly cast them off. Beside vv. 13–16 it gives the same two-sided answer, refusal and then mercy.

Surviving copies of Josephus skip Tola altogether, which his translator Whiston took to be a loss in the manuscripts. Jair's thirty donkey-riding sons become skilled horsemen entrusted with governing the cities of Gilead. Josephus then compresses vv. 6–16: Israel's affairs fell into disorder and contempt of God, Ammon and the Philistines laid the country waste, and the Hebrews, chastened, offered sacrifices and begged God to leave off his anger. The LORD's refusal and Israel's second confession are left out, so the turn comes from sacrifice rather than from putting away the gods.

Makes Jair an apostate. He builds a sanctuary to Baal and decrees death for anyone who will not sacrifice. Seven men refuse, recalling Deborah's charge to keep the law, and Jair orders them burned, but Nathaniel, the angel over fire, rescues them and burns Jair's servants, then Jair himself with the pillar of Baal and a thousand men. Judges says nothing against Jair; the retelling supplies a cause for the apostasy of v. 6, and its translator, Montague James, heard echoes of the furnace in Daniel 3.

When Ammon takes their cities, the people gather at Mizpeh (Masphath) and say the Lord has departed from them. Then all of them, men and women, boys and sucklings, pray “spoil not the vine which thy right hand hath planted,” and God repents of his anger and strengthens Jephthah's spirit. The curt exchange of vv. 10–16 becomes a full public prayer and an explicit change of heart. Jephthah, in the same retelling, urges the people to set their hearts on the law before they fight.

Counts the two lists that sit a few verses apart: seven nations the LORD saved Israel from (vv. 11–12) and seven gods Israel served (v. 6). In this reading Israel owed God seven praises for seven deliverances and repaid him with seven idols. The midrash pairs the complaint with Micah 6:3, “O my people, what have I done unto thee?” and goes on to say God asked nothing hard of them, only offerings from the animals they already had.

Takes the end of v. 6, “and served not him,” to mean Israel did not serve the LORD even alongside the other gods. Rabbi Yose bar Hanina has God say he would have settled for being worshiped last, like the dessert after a meal. The same passage claims Damascus had a shrine for every day of the year, and that Israel made all those gods its masters together.

David Kimhi notes that Tola rose “to save Israel” after Abimelech and argues that the phrase implies Abimelech also saved Israel from its enemies, or he would not be counted this way. He also reports that some copies of the Targum render “son of Dodo” as son of his father's brother, which would make Tola a cousin of Abimelech. That reading would tie him to Gideon's family, though v. 1 calls Tola a man of Issachar and Gideon's clan was in Manasseh (6:15), a puzzle Augustine also tried to solve.

On “his soul was grieved” (v. 16) Rashi writes that God, as it were, could not contain his pain at Israel's misery, as if he lacked the room to bear it. The Targum keeps the human picture too, saying his soul was distressed by Israel's affliction, where it often softens such language about God.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Judges 10:16; Targum Jonathan on Judges 10:16

traditions.text: Augustine's Latin Bible calls Tola son of his father's brother, the reading Radak found in some Targum copies, and he takes on the same puzzle: how could Abimelech's uncle be a man of Issachar when Gideon was of Manasseh? He suggests Gideon and Puah had one mother by different fathers, since women married across tribes. He cites Saul giving his Benjamite daughter to David of Judah, and Elizabeth, a daughter of Aaron, as kin of Mary.

11.overview:
Jephthah, a harlot's son driven out by his half-brothers, leads a band of raiders in Tob until Gilead's elders, desperate against Ammon, agree to make him their head. He argues Israel's right to the land in a long message to Ammon's king, who will not listen. Then the Spirit of the LORD comes on him, and he vows that whatever comes out of his door to meet him on his return will be the LORD's, offered as a burnt offering. He wins, and his only child, a daughter, comes out dancing to meet him.

The text is plain about the vow and spare about its keeping. Jephthah promised a burnt offering (v. 31) and said he could not go back (v. 35). After two months of mourning her virginity, he “did with her according to his vow,” and “she knew no man” (v. 39). No altar is described, and nothing in the text says he did other than he vowed.

11.hermeneutics:
Border quarrels between neighbors were argued from history and from the gods. About 2400 BC Enmetena, ruler of Lagash in southern Mesopotamia, recorded his city's long dispute with Umma over the fields between them. His inscription begins with the god Enlil fixing the border between the gods of the two cities, tells how a king of Kish measured it and set up a stone marker, and then lists each time Umma's rulers crossed it and how Lagash answered. Jephthah's message (vv. 15–27) works the same way: a record of who held the land and for how long, a claim that each people keeps what its god gave it (v. 24), and an appeal to a divine judge to decide (v. 27).

The wording of the vow fits the houses of the time. The best-preserved Iron Age I house yet found in the Levant, at Tall al-'Umayri near modern Amman, was rebuilt about 1150 BC with two rows of pillars dividing a ground floor that stabled animals and stored food, with living space above. In a house like that an animal could well be the first thing through the door. Readers have long asked whether Jephthah expected an animal or a person. His Hebrew allows either “whatever” or “whoever,” and the one who comes out “to meet him” is his daughter (v. 34).
