structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the outcast's return to the price of his victory.

rows.text: The outcast made head of Gilead

notes: **Words that bind:** the bargain with the elders is spoken “before the LORD in Mizpeh” (v. 11), and both Jephthah and his daughter say he has “opened” his mouth to the LORD (vv. 35, 36).

**Return:** the verb *shuv* comes 6 times: the elders turn back to him (v. 8), he asks to be brought back (v. 9), Ammon demands the land back (v. 13), he vows on his return (v. 31), cannot go back (v. 35), and she returns to him (v. 39).
**Possess:** the verb for taking possession comes 8 times in vv. 21–24, the heart of his case.
**The Judge:** Jephthah leaves the case to “the LORD the Judge” (v. 27); no named judge in the book is given that title.

Chapter 11 is the center of the Jephthah section (10:1–12:15). It answers 10:18 directly: the “head” Gilead wanted becomes Jephthah's price (vv. 8–11). It runs straight on into 12:1, where Ephraim complains that he crossed over to fight without them.

**Echoes:** his daughter is his only child (v. 34), the word used of Isaac in Genesis 22:2, where another father is told to offer a burnt offering and is stopped. Samuel later lists Jephthah among the deliverers the LORD sent (1 Samuel 12:11).

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church's Bible Dictionary says Jephthah is known chiefly for a rash vow, which led him to offer his own daughter in sacrifice. It adds that Hebrews 11:32 commends him, probably for delivering Israel from Ammon. The Church's published reference takes the plain reading of v. 39.

A thematic link. Abraham describes the priest of Pharaoh in Chaldea offering men, women and children to strange gods, among them three virgins, the daughters of Onitah, killed on the altar because they would not worship gods of wood or stone. In Restoration scripture the offering of a daughter belongs to idolatry, the practice Deuteronomy 12:31 condemns when it says the nations burned “their sons and their daughters” to their gods.

Josephus has Jephthah vow to sacrifice “what living creature soever should first meet him,” and states the outcome plainly: he sacrificed his daughter as a burnt offering. Josephus judges the act sharply, an offering neither in keeping with the law nor acceptable to God. He makes the daughter willing, content to die for her father's victory and her people's freedom.

Here God is angry at the vow itself: if a dog met Jephthah first, would a dog be offered to the Lord? So the vow will fall on his firstborn, his only daughter, and God will save Israel anyway, for the people's prayer and not for Jephthah's sake.

Gives the daughter a name, Seila, and a voice. She recalls Isaac, who did not resist his father, and fears her death will be wasted unless she offers herself willingly. On the mountain she laments the wedding she will never have, her mother's white robe and her nurse's crown of flowers. Her father does all he vowed, the maidens bury her, and Israel mourns her four days a year at a tomb called by her name.

The Aramaic translation reads v. 39 as a sacrifice and turns the “custom” into a decree: from then on no one in Israel was to offer up a son or daughter as a burnt offering, as Jephthah did. It adds that he did not consult Phinehas the priest, who could have redeemed her with money.

Counts Jephthah among those who asked God improperly, since an unclean animal might have come out first, and says God answered him improperly with his daughter. It then reads Jeremiah 19:5, burnt offerings “which I commanded not, nor spake it,” as covering three cases, and takes “nor spake it” as Jephthah's sacrifice of his daughter.

Kimhi grants that the rabbis held she was sacrificed, then gives his father Joseph Kimhi's reading: the “and” of v. 31 means “or,” so what came out would be holy to the LORD if unfit for the altar, or a burnt offering if fit. On this view Jephthah built her a house where she lived apart, and the daughters of Israel went yearly to talk with and console her. Kimhi calls it the plain sense, since she mourned her virginity, not her life, and v. 39 says “she knew no man” without saying he offered her.

Names Jephthah, with Gideon, Barak and Samson, among those who “through faith subdued kingdoms” (v. 33). The letter says nothing of the vow, and Christian readers after it had to set this praise beside v. 39, as the next entries show.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose says Jephthah vowed without thought and repented when his daughter came out; he cannot blame him for keeping the vow, but calls it a wretched necessity solved only by her death. Better not to vow, he concludes, than to vow what God does not wish paid, and the ram given for Isaac shows what God wants. He ranks the daughter's constancy above that of two Pythagorean friends famous for being ready to die for each other.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 3.12.78–81; cf. 1.50.264

traditions.text: Answering pagans who called the story cruel, Chrysostom says God let the sacrifice go forward out of care: had he stopped it, others would have made such vows expecting him to intervene, and child murder would have multiplied. After this, he says, no one vowed such a vow again. He reports that Israel's virgins mourned her forty days a year, where Judges says four.

Jovinian had ranked the father's faith above his daughter's tears. Jerome answers that most Hebrews blame Jephthah for a rash vow, asking what he would have done if a dog or an ass had met him. In their view, he reports, God ordered events so that a man who vowed carelessly learned his error by his daughter's death.

Augustine thinks Jephthah meant a person from the start: livestock did not run out to meet generals coming home from war, a dog would have been unclean, and his Latin text reads “whoever.” Scripture, he notes, passes no verdict on the vow, as with Judah and Tamar, and leaves readers to weigh it. He concludes that Jephthah took his daughter's coming as God's punishment and submitted, and that Israel's yearly mourning shows it was no vow of joy, so that no one would dare make one like it again.

On v. 24 Augustine asks whether Jephthah grants that Chemosh really gave Ammon its land. He reads the line as spoken from the king's point of view, what Chemosh gives you as you suppose, while the LORD truly drove the Amorites out and gave their land to Israel. He weighs and sets aside the idea that Chemosh might be the angel set over Ammon.

12.overview:
The men of Ephraim cross the Jordan and threaten to burn Jephthah's house over him because he fought Ammon without them. Jephthah answers that he called and they did not come, then leads Gilead against them. Gilead seizes the fords, and every fugitive who asks to cross is told to say *shibboleth*; whoever says “sibboleth” is killed. Forty-two thousand Ephraimites fall. Jephthah judges six years and dies. Three minor judges follow: Ibzan of Bethlehem, with thirty sons and thirty daughters; Elon of Zebulun; and Abdon of Pirathon, whose forty sons and thirty grandsons ride seventy donkeys.

Notice the fords. Ehud's men and Gideon's seized the fords of the Jordan to cut off foreign enemies (3:28; 7:24). Here Israelites hold them against Israelites, and the way a man says one word decides whether he lives.

12.hermeneutics:
The test at the fords rests on a real difference in speech. *Shibboleth* can mean an ear of grain or a flowing stream. Since E. A. Speiser's study of 1942, a common explanation is that the Gileadites east of the Jordan kept an old Semitic sound, the *th* of English “thin,” in this word, while Ephraimites west of the river lacked it and could only come out with an *s*. Support came from Ammon, Gilead's neighbor: a seal found at Tall al-'Umayri names an Ammonite king Ba'alyasha, a name built on a root with that same sound, and Jeremiah 40:14 spells him Baalis. Scholars still debate the exact sounds, but v. 6 shows that Hebrew was spoken with regional accents, and that an accent could mark a man as an enemy.

Ibzan's thirty daughters sent out and thirty brides brought in (v. 9) describe marriage as policy. At Mari on the Euphrates in the 18th century BC, King Zimri-Lim married several daughters to the rulers of vassal towns, and his letters show the results. Two of them, Shimatum and Kirum, went to the same vassal, Haya-Sumu of Ilan-sura; the sisters became rivals, and Kirum was divorced and sent home to Mari. A man with sixty children married outside his clan had sixty ties to other houses. The book records Ibzan's family the way Mari records a king's, as a measure of his reach.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, a civil war and then three judges in a fixed formula.
notes: **Pass over:** the verb comes 8 times from 11:29 to 12:5. Jephthah passed over to Ammon (11:29, 32), Ephraim complains he passed over without them (12:1, 3), and the fleeing Ephraimites beg, “Let me go over” (v. 5).
**Fugitives:** the taunt of v. 4, that Gileadites are “fugitives of Ephraim,” returns in v. 5, where the same Hebrew phrase names the Ephraimites who “were escaped.”

**Formula:** each minor judge gets a name, a home, years, a death and a burial; “buried” comes 6 times in 10:1–12:15, for Tola, Jair, Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon and Abdon. Abdon's 70 riders (v. 14, KJV “nephews” for grandsons) echo Jair's 30 sons on 30 colts (10:4).

Chapter 12 closes the Jephthah section (10:1–12:15). The war with Ephraim ends Jephthah's story, and three minor judges balance Tola and Jair at its start. Then 13:1 returns to the full cycle with the Philistines, the second oppressor named in 10:7.
**Backward:** Ephraim made the same complaint to Gideon (8:1–3), and his soft answer calmed them. Jephthah answers sharply, and the quarrel ends in slaughter.

traditions.text: Josephus has Jephthah tell Ephraim they should have come even before they were invited, and that men without courage to face the enemy were hurrying against their own kin. His Jephthah also threatens punishment, with God's help, unless Ephraim grows wiser. Josephus keeps the slaughter at the passages of Jordan, about forty-two thousand, but leaves out the password. He buries Jephthah in his own country at a place called Sebee, has Ibzan leave all sixty children alive and married, and makes Abdon's seventy descendants skilled riders of horses instead of donkeys.

Skips the war with Ephraim and has Jephthah judge ten years instead of six. Abdon, called Addo of Praton, fights a war Judges does not mention: Moab demands its cities back, as Ammon did, and Addo routs it and kills 45,000. Elon then judges twenty years instead of ten and takes twelve Philistine cities, so the quiet judges become warriors. The Moabite demand repeats Ammon's claim of 11:13 almost word for word, and Addo's answer points back to what happened to Ammon.

Explains an oddity in v. 7: the Hebrew says Jephthah was buried “in the cities of Gilead,” plural. He was punished for his daughter's death, the midrash says, with a disease that made his limbs fall off one by one wherever he went, and each was buried where it fell. Rashi repeats the story in his comment on 11:39, where he also blames Jephthah for not seeking release from the vow. The burial note of v. 7, read this way, becomes the end of the story of the vow.

David Kimhi gives that midrash as the homiletic reading of v. 7, then the plain one: the plural means one of the cities of Gilead, just as Saul's offer to make David his son-in-law “in the one of the twain” (1 Samuel 18:21) means one of two daughters. He adds Zechariah 9:9, where the king's colt is literally the foal of “she-asses” yet means the foal of one, so a plural noun can point to a single member of a group. The KJV's rendering of v. 7 follows this plain sense, where the midrash builds its story on the plural.

On the password, Kimhi suggests the Gileadites could have used any word with the letter shin, since the Ephraimites read it as samekh, and the text records one example. Perhaps the air of their land caused it, he says, as the people of France cannot say shin and pronounce it like a soft *t*. He treats the test as a matter of regional accent, the same direction modern linguists take (see Hermeneutics).

Finds the password foretold in Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh. The Hebrew verb for “grow into a multitude” in Genesis 48:16 is built on the word for fish, and the midrash says Jacob was hinting that Ephraim's descendants would be caught like fish. Fish are caught by the mouth, and the Ephraimites at the fords were caught by the way they pronounced one word (v. 6).

Rashi takes *shibboleth* in its sense of a stream, so the man at the ford asks, in effect, to cross the current. Following the Targum, he reads v. 4 as a taunt: the lowliest of Ephraim mocked Gilead as a nobody among Ephraim and Manasseh. He says the Ephraimites simply had a speech defect, where Radak blames the climate.

Rabbah bar Rav Huna, citing Rav, identifies the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem with Boaz, the husband of Ruth. Boaz made two wedding feasts for each of his sixty children, one in each family's house, and never invited the childless Manoah, Samson's father, since he could not return the favor. All sixty died in his lifetime; the one son born from Ruth outweighed them.

Augustine closes his long discussion of Jephthah with a figurative reading of this chapter. If the defeat of Ephraim points to the last judgment, the number is not idle: forty-two thousand is six times seven, matching the six ages of the world, as the daughter's two months, sixty days, did. Jephthah's six years as judge (v. 7), he adds, are no accident either. He offers it tentatively, after defending the plain story.

13.overview:
Israel does evil again, and the Philistines rule it for forty years. In Zorah, a town of Dan, the angel of the LORD appears to Manoah’s childless wife. She will bear a son who is to be a Nazarite from the womb, so she must drink no wine and eat nothing unclean, and the boy “shall begin to deliver Israel.” Manoah prays for the visitor to return. He comes again, to the woman in the field, repeats his instructions, declines a meal, and will not give his name. When Manoah offers a kid on a rock, the angel goes up in the flame of the altar. The son is born and named Samson, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to move him.

Watch who understands. The woman, never named, meets the angel both times, keeps his instructions, and answers her husband’s fear of death with plain reasoning (v. 23). Manoah asks the questions and understands last.

13.hermeneutics:
Egypt told the births of some kings as announced by the gods. On the walls of Hatshepsut’s temple at Deir el-Bahri (15th century BC), the god Thoth brings Amun to Queen Ahmose, Amun tells her she will bear a ruler of Upper and Lower Egypt, and the potter god Khnum shapes the child on his wheel. Amenhotep III had the same cycle carved at Luxor. The scenes made a ruler legitimate by giving him a divine father. Judges 13 keeps the announcement to the mother and nothing else. The child has a human father and is no king, in a book whose refrain is that Israel had no king (17:6). What the angel brings is a rule of life for mother and son and a limited charge: the boy will only “begin” to deliver Israel (v. 5).

In the Ugaritic myths the gods send word by messengers, such as Baal’s pair Gupan and Ugar, who bow before the one they visit and deliver their master’s words as his. An envoy in that world stood in for his sender, and the courtesy shown to him was shown through him to the one who sent him. Manoah follows the custom. He offers the stranger a kid and asks his name so that he can honor him “when thy sayings come to pass” (v. 17). The scene turns on how fully this messenger stands in for his sender. He will not eat, he directs the offering to the LORD, and when he vanishes in the flame Manoah concludes, “we have seen God” (v. 22).

Meal refused, name withheld, ascent in the flame

notes: **The unnamed woman:** she is “the woman” or “his wife” 14 times, while Manoah is named 17 times. It is she who gives the child his name (v. 24).
**Name:** the word comes 5 times: Manoah’s name (v. 2), the name the visitor did not tell (v. 6), Manoah’s question and the refusal (vv. 17–18), and Samson’s naming (v. 24).

**Wonder:** the angel calls his name *peli*, “secret” or “wonderful” (v. 18), and in the next verse he “did wondrously,” a verb from the same root. The answer to Manoah’s question is shown in the fire.

Chapters 13–16 are the last and longest deliverer story in Judges. They open with the book’s familiar formula, Israel “did evil again” and is handed over (v. 1), but this time no one cries out to the LORD, the step that starts the earlier cycles (3:9; 6:6; 10:10). Samson is promised before anyone asks.

**Backward and forward:** Zorah and Eshtaol reappear when Dan sends spies to find new land (18:2). A barren woman’s son with no razor on his head returns in Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11), under whom the Philistines are finally subdued (1 Samuel 7:13).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 3, where the angel appears to Manoah’s wife, points to Mormon’s sermon on faith, hope, and charity. Mormon asks whether angels have ceased to minister and answers no: they show themselves “unto them of strong faith and a firm mind.” Their office, he says, is to call people to repentance and prepare the way for faith in Christ.

The Church’s footnote to v. 1, “did evil again,” points first to King Benjamin’s words about Lehi’s family in the wilderness. When they were unfaithful, he says, they did not prosper or progress in their journey but were driven back and smitten with famine and sore afflictions “to stir them up in remembrance of their duty.” The footnote sets Israel’s forty years under the Philistines beside that kind of affliction; it also cites Helaman 12:2–3, Mormon’s comment on the same pattern.

Josephus makes Manoah the leading man of his district and his wife famous for her beauty. The angel appears as a tall, handsome young man, and when the wife praises him, Manoah’s jealousy flares; she prays for the angel to come back so her husband’s suspicion can be cleared. The angel touches the meat with his rod, fire breaks out, and he rises to heaven on the smoke. The name Samson, Josephus says, means “one that is strong.”

This Jewish retelling of biblical history names the wife Eluma, daughter of Remac. Manoah tells her day after day that the Lord has shut her womb and asks to take another wife; she replies that the fault is his. She goes up alone to an upper room and prays to learn which of them is barren, and the angel tells her it is she, but that her prayer is heard. The angel who came, it adds, was named Phadahel.

Records that Samson’s mother was named Tzlelponit and his sister Nashyan. Asked what difference such names make, it answers that they give a reply to sectarians who press for details the Bible does not supply: there is a received tradition. Pseudo-Philo’s Eluma shows the same wish to name her, in a different line of tradition.

Rav Nahman takes v. 11, where Manoah “went after his wife,” to show that he was an unlearned man, since a man should not walk behind a woman. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objects that similar words are used of Elkanah and of Elisha, so the phrase must mean that Manoah followed her counsel. The disagreement is about the question the chapter itself raises: who is leading?

Asks what “unclean thing” in v. 4 can mean, since Manoah’s wife would not have eaten forbidden food anyway; Rabbi Yitzhak answers that it means things forbidden to a Nazarite. On v. 25, where the Spirit began “to move him,” the Talmud hears the word for the bells on the high priest’s robe (Exodus 39:26): the Divine Presence rang before Samson like a bell.

Rabbi Yohanan says Samson’s name, from the word for sun, echoes a name of God: “the LORD God is a sun and shield” (Psalm 84:11). As God shields the world, Samson shielded Israel in his generation. Rabbi Hama son of Hanina reads the promise that the boy would begin to deliver Israel (v. 5) as the end of an old oath: the Philistines had broken the covenant their king Abimelech made with Abraham (Genesis 21:23).

The Aramaic translation of the Prophets softens the meeting with God. The woman reports a prophet of the Lord rather than a man of God (v. 6), and Manoah fears death because “we have seen an angel of the Lord,” where the Hebrew has “God” (v. 22). The angel’s name is simply “wondrous” (v. 18).

Explains why the angel withholds his name: it is concealed because it keeps changing, so that no one name holds from day to day. On Jacob’s wrestler, who answers Jacob with nearly the same question (Genesis 32:29, the verse the Church’s footnote to v. 18 cites), Rashi says angels have no fixed names, which change with each errand. Pseudo-Philo, by contrast, supplies the name.

Writing to a new bishop, Vigilius, about marriage outside the faith, Ambrose retells Samson’s life from the beginning. He praises the mother as barren in body but fruitful in virtue, a woman who would not keep the angel’s promise from her husband. He rejects the view of “one writer,” Josephus, that Manoah asked for the angel’s return out of jealousy; Manoah wanted to share the vision.

Ambrose opens his second book on the Holy Spirit with the judges as proof that the Spirit worked in Israel. Samson, “born by the divine promise,” had the Spirit with him from v. 25 on, and Ambrose credits his strength to that guidance alone. He adds a wish: that Samson had been as careful to keep grace as he was strong against the lion.

14.overview:
Samson goes down to Timnath, sees a Philistine woman, and tells his parents to get her for him. They object to a wife from “the uncircumcised Philistines,” but the narrator adds that the LORD was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, who ruled Israel. On the way Samson tears apart a young lion with his bare hands; later he finds bees and honey in its carcass, eats, and tells no one. At the wedding feast he sets thirty Philistine companions a riddle, with thirty garments as the stake. They threaten to burn his bride’s family, she weeps on him for seven days, and he tells her. She tells them. Samson pays the wager with garments stripped from thirty men he kills at Ashkelon, and his wife is given to his companion.

Notice the secret. Samson hides the lion from his parents (vv. 6, 9) and from his guests, and the chapter turns on who is told and who tells.

14.hermeneutics:
Timnah is Tel Batash in the Sorek valley, about 7 km northwest of Beth-shemesh, excavated by George Kelm and Amihai Mazar from 1977 to 1989. In the Philistine era it was a fortified town of close-packed mud-brick houses. At Beth-shemesh itself, a few kilometers from Zorah, excavators Shlomo Bunimovitz and Zvi Lederman announced in 2012 a stone seal about 15 mm across from the early Iron Age, showing a man beside a large animal, most likely a lion. They did not say the man was Samson. They argued that a story of a man meeting a lion was already told in this border valley between Israelites and Philistines. Samson’s first feat (vv. 5–6) belongs to that landscape, and it happens on the road through the Philistines’ own vineyards.

Many ancient writers believed that bees could be born from a dead animal. Virgil, writing about 29 BC, tells how Aristaeus lost his hives, sacrificed bulls, and on the ninth day saw bees swarm from their rotted bodies (*Georgics* 4.554–558). Samson’s riddle rests on that kind of sight, one his hearers would have thought marvelous but not absurd: food out of the eater, sweetness out of the strong.

Riddles were a feasting game with stakes. Athenaeus (c. AD 200) gathers Greek lore on riddles at drinking parties and quotes Clearchus of Soli (c. 300 BC), who defined the riddle as a problem posed in jest for a prize or a forfeit; at Athens a loser drank brine mixed into his wine. Samson’s contest at a seven-day feast follows the form, with prize and forfeit fixed before the riddle is heard (vv. 12–13). His riddle breaks the rules of the game, because no one could solve it without having seen what only Samson saw.

notes: **Telling:** the verb *nagad*, “tell” or “declare,” comes 14 times. Samson tells his parents about the woman (v. 2) but not the lion (vv. 6, 9), refuses his wife (v. 16), then tells her, and she tells her people (v. 17).
**Riddle:** the noun comes 8 times and the matching verb, “put forth” a riddle, 3 times, all in vv. 12–19.

**Down and seven:** the verb “go down” comes 5 times, toward Timnath and at last to Ashkelon. The feast lasts seven days, the guests are stumped for three, and everything breaks on “the seventh day” (vv. 15, 17, 18).

Chapter 14 opens a run of Philistine clashes that all grow from Samson’s Timnite marriage: the riddle (ch. 14), the burned fields (15:1–8), and the battle at Lehi (15:9–20), closed by the formula in 15:20. Verse 4 is the narrator’s key to the whole run: the LORD was seeking an occasion against the Philistines.

**Forward:** Samson’s reason in v. 3, “she pleaseth me well,” is in Hebrew “she is right in my eyes,” the words of the book’s closing refrain, “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25). Delilah’s pressing in 16:15–17 replays the bride’s in vv. 16–17.

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 6, where the Spirit of the LORD comes on Samson before he tears the lion apart, points to Nephi bound by his brothers in the wilderness. Nephi prays for strength to “burst these bands with which I am bound,” and the bands fall from his hands and feet, after which he speaks to his brothers again. The footnote links two scenes in which power comes on a threatened man; Nephi’s follows a prayer of faith.

Josephus has the parents refuse because the woman is not of Israel, then adds that the marriage was of God, who meant to turn it to the Hebrews’ good. The Timnites give Samson thirty companions out of fear, as a guard disguised as friends. He brings the bride three honeycombs. Josephus words the riddle as a great devourer that produced sweet food out of itself, though itself very disagreeable, and when it is solved Samson answers that nothing is more deceitful than a woman, since one had betrayed him.

Citing the Tosefta, the Talmud says Samson “rebelled with his eyes”: he wanted the woman because she was right in his eyes (v. 3), and so the Philistines put out his eyes (16:21). It then raises v. 4, which says the match was of the LORD, and answers that God used the marriage against the Philistines, but Samson himself went after his own desire and not for the sake of heaven.

Judges says Samson “went down” to Timnath (v. 1), but Genesis says Judah “goeth up” there (Genesis 38:13). Rabbi Elazar reads the verbs morally: Samson was disgraced at Timnah, so he goes down, and Judah was raised up there, so he goes up. Others propose two towns named Timnah, or a single town on a slope, reached by going down from one side and up from the other.

The Aramaic translation turns Samson’s barbed reply into plain speech: had you not searched the matter out through my wife, you would not have found my riddle (v. 18). Where the Hebrew says the Spirit of the LORD came upon him (vv. 6, 19), it says a spirit of might from before the Lord rested on him, its usual way of naming the strength of the judges.

Passes over the lion, the honey, and the riddle entirely. It says only that when Samson began to grow up and sought to fight against the Philistines, he took a Philistine wife, whom they later burned with fire because he had brought them so low. In this retelling the marriage serves the war from the start, as v. 4 suggests, and the details of chs. 14–15 are left to the book of Judges, which it names (43:4).

In his code of Jewish law, Maimonides insists that Samson did not marry a woman who stayed a gentile. His wives converted, but for his sake and without a court, so Scripture treats them as if they were still foreign, and their later conduct showed what their motives had been. He sets Samson beside Solomon, whose foreign wives turned away his heart (1 Kings 11:4). The ruling answers the question v. 3 raises, how a man raised up by God could marry outside Israel, by placing the fault in a conversion done for the wrong reasons.

Ambrose reads the episode as a mystery of the Church. The roaring lion torn apart is the once-savage people of the Gentiles, who now have honey as the people of Christ, and the riddle that stayed unsolved for three days was answered on the seventh, as the apostles understood only after the Passion. He also reports another reading, in which the slain lion is Christ, the lion of Judah, in whose body the bees of the Church store the honey of wisdom.

In the letter to Vigilius the marriage is the start of Samson’s ruin. Ambrose pictures the young men at the feast, stirred by the banquet, provoking each other with jests and questions as was usual at such times. When the riddle is solved, he gives Samson the line Josephus adds, “Nor is ought more treacherous than a woman,” and makes the whole story a warning to Christians against marrying outside the faith.

15.overview:
At wheat harvest Samson comes with a kid to visit his wife and learns that her father has given her to his companion; he is offered her younger sister instead. Samson ties three hundred foxes tail to tail with torches between them and turns them loose in the Philistines’ grain, vineyards, and olive groves. The Philistines burn his wife and her father. He strikes them down and retreats to the rock Etam. When a Philistine force camps at Lehi, three thousand men of Judah bind him with new cords and hand him over. The cords melt like burnt flax, and with a fresh jawbone of a donkey he kills a thousand men. Parched, he calls on the LORD, and water breaks out at Lehi.

Follow the reprisals. Each side justifies itself by what the other did (vv. 3, 7, 10–11), until Samson’s own people bind him. Only at the end does he call on the LORD.

15.hermeneutics:
Ovid’s *Fasti* (about AD 8) explains a strange custom at Rome’s festival of Ceres in April: foxes were let loose in the Circus with burning torches tied to their backs. His host from Carseoli told him the reason. A farm boy caught a vixen that had raided the henyard, wrapped her in straw and hay, and set it alight; she escaped and ran through the ripe fields, and the wind spread the fire through the crop. A local law afterward banned foxes. The story shows how farmers pictured a fire-carrying animal in standing grain: the loss of a year’s harvest. Samson strikes at the driest point of the year, the wheat harvest (v. 1), and the narrator counts what burns, shocks and standing grain, vineyards and olive trees (v. 5).

Ancient law treated field fires as a wrong with a price. The Hittite laws (c. 1650–1100 BC) say that if someone sets fire to a field and it catches a vineyard in fruit, he pays six shekels of silver for every vine or fruit tree and replants them; one who carries embers into his field and burns a neighbor’s ripening crop must take the burnt field and give the owner a good one (§§105–106). Exodus 22:6, which the Church’s footnote to v. 5 cites, makes “he that kindled the fire” pay restitution. In that world someone always answered for a fire. The Philistines go after the household they blame (v. 6), and the men of Judah, who live under Philistine rule, take the penalty as falling on them (vv. 10–11).

rows.text: The bride withheld: fire, reprisal, slaughter

notes: **Tit for tat:** the Philistines come “to do to him as he hath done to us” (v. 10), and Samson answers, “As they did unto me, so have I done unto them” (v. 11). Verses 3 and 7 give his reasons in the same spirit.

**Bind and hand:** “bind” comes 5 times, all in vv. 10–13, and “hand” 7 times in vv. 12–18, from Judah’s plan to deliver Samson into the Philistines’ hand to his fear of falling into “the hand of the uncircumcised.”
**Jaw:** *lehi* means “jaw” and is also the place’s name; it comes 8 times in vv. 9–19. In v. 19 the Hebrew can be read either way (see Traditions).

Chapter 15 finishes the Timnite story begun in 14:1 and closes the first part of Samson’s life with a formula: “he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years” (v. 20). Chapter 16 then adds a second story and repeats the formula (16:31).

**Backward:** Judah, the tribe told to “go up” first against the Canaanites (1:2), now goes up against its own deliverer to hand him over. An earlier judge, Shamgar, also struck the Philistines with a farm tool, six hundred with an ox goad (3:31).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to “loosed” in v. 14 points to two Book of Mormon scenes. In Alma 2 the Nephites, “strengthened by the hand of the Lord” after praying mightily, defeat the Amlicites and Lamanites. In Alma 14, Alma and Amulek, bound in prison, pray for strength according to their faith in Christ, break the cords that bind them, and walk out as the walls fall on their captors. In both, the strength follows a prayer, while in Judges 15 Samson prays only after the battle (v. 18).

Josephus says the fields were nearly ripe when the foxes went in, and has the men of Judah protest that they pay their tribute and still suffer for Samson’s deeds. The place of the battle, he adds, had no name until Samson’s feat gave it the name the Jaw-bone, which it still bore in his day. Samson then boasted that the victory came from his own courage, not from God’s help. The thirst that followed taught him that human courage is nothing, and he begged God not to hold his words against him; God then opened a spring of sweet water at a rock.

Why foxes? Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explains that a fox doubles back when it flees, so Samson chose it to punish the Philistines, who had gone back on the oath their king Abimelech swore to Abraham (Genesis 21:23). The same broken oath appears in the Talmud’s reading of 13:5, so the fire in the fields becomes the penalty for a broken covenant. On the same page Rabbi Yohanan says Samson judged Israel (v. 20) as their Father in heaven does, applying “Dan shall judge his people” (Genesis 49:16) to him.

Rabbi Yitzhak of the school of Rabbi Ami ties the water of v. 19 to Samson’s character. Samson had craved something unclean, the Philistine women, so his life was saved through something unclean, the jawbone of a donkey. The Talmud draws the same measure-for-measure lesson from his eyes (16:21).

The Aramaic translation reads v. 19 as a miracle of the place, not of the bone: the Lord split the rock that was in Lehi, and water came out of it. It names the spring for Samson’s prayer, “the Spring that was Given through the Prayer of Samson.” Josephus also brings the water from a rock, and the Church’s footnote offers the same alternative: God opened the basin at Lehi.

Rashi keeps the jaw. The “hollow place” of v. 19 is literally a mortar, and he explains it as the socket in the jawbone where a tooth is set, shaped like a mortar. En-hakkore, in his reading, is the spring that came through the cry of the one who called to the LORD. His reading stands opposite the Targum’s, and it is the one the KJV follows with “the jaw.”

Ambrose finds a lesson in the foxes: the cunning of those who fight against divine mysteries burns their own harvest, and he joins them to the little foxes that spoil the vines (Song of Solomon 2:15). The water from the jawbone he takes either as plain miracle or as a figure of the Gentiles’ humility, linking the jaw to the cheek turned to the one who strikes it (Matthew 5:39). Samson stayed unconquered, he says, as long as he kept the grace of the Spirit.

Ambrose gives Samson a speech to the three thousand men of Judah, rebuking them for becoming servants of other men’s insolence and turning their arms against themselves. Like Josephus he faults Samson after the victory: he took the glory, named the place for his own feat, and built no altar. Thirst taught him that human strength fails without God, and his prayer made amends, so that “arrogance soon incurs offence” while humility gains reconciliation.

A church prayer in this collection asks God to accept the prayers of Christians as he accepted those of the righteous in every generation, and lists them: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Gideon at the rock, Manoah and his wife in the field, and Samson “in his thirst before the transgression.” It counts v. 18 as an answered prayer and places it before his later sin; Gideon and Jephthah are each qualified the same way.

16.overview:
At Gaza Samson goes in to a harlot. The men of the city wait at the gate to kill him at dawn, but at midnight he pulls up the doors, posts, and bar and carries them to a hill near Hebron. Then he loves Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and the Philistine lords pay her to learn the secret of his strength. Three times he gives a false answer. The fourth time he tells her about the razor, and while he sleeps his seven locks are shaved. The LORD leaves him; the Philistines put out his eyes and set him grinding in the prison at Gaza. At a feast for Dagon they bring him out for sport. Samson prays, pushes the two middle pillars, and the house falls on the lords and on himself.

Notice v. 20. Samson expects to shake himself free “as at other times,” and “wist not that the LORD was departed from him.”

16.hermeneutics:
Dagon was not a god the Philistines brought with them. Dagan was an old god of inland Syria, worshipped long before them at Tuttul and Terqa on the middle Euphrates, in the archives of Mari and Ebla, and later at Emar, where he heads the offering lists. Texts of that region call him father of the gods, and at Ugarit Baal is called his son. No Philistine inscription names him; the Bible alone makes him their chief god, with houses at Gaza and at Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:2). The newcomers on the coast had taken up a god long honored in the land they settled. The old idea of a fish-god comes from medieval interpreters and is now set aside. When the lords credit Dagon with Samson’s capture (vv. 23–24), the contest is between the LORD and a god of the whole region.

At Tell Qasile, inside modern Tel Aviv, Amihai Mazar excavated (1971–74) a Philistine temple rebuilt several times over the 12th and 11th centuries BC. In its last phase the roof of the main hall rested on two cedar posts set on round stone bases along the center line, about two meters apart. Offering vessels lay on the floors and around the raised platform. A hall whose roof hangs on two central posts explains why the story speaks of “the two middle pillars upon which the house stood” (v. 29), and why people standing on the roof (v. 27) would come down with it. The Qasile temple is small; the house at Gaza in Judges holds the lords below and about three thousand people above.

Seven locks woven into the web

notes: **Refrain:** each round ends with “The Philistines be upon thee, Samson” (vv. 9, 12, 14, 20). The fourth time there is no strength behind his waking.
**Bind:** the verb comes 12 times, from the lords’ plan in v. 5 to the bronze fetters of v. 21, counting the “prison house,” in Hebrew the house of the bound (vv. 21, 25). “Strength” comes 7 times.

**Knowing and once:** v. 9 ends “his strength was not known,” and v. 20 “he wist not,” the same verb. Delilah calls the lords to come “this once” (v. 18); Samson asks God for strength “only this once” (v. 28), the same Hebrew word.

Chapter 16 is a second Samson story set after the closing formula of 15:20. It ends with his burial between Zorah and Eshtaol, where the Spirit first moved him (13:25), and the formula again: “he judged Israel twenty years” (v. 31). It also ends the book’s deliverer stories; chapters 17–21 have no judge.
**Forward:** Dagon’s house appears again when the Philistines set the captured ark beside his image at Ashdod, and the god is found fallen on his face before it (1 Samuel 5:2–3).

traditions.text: A thematic link to vv. 17 and 20, not a Church footnote. Mormon describes Nephites who, through pride and wickedness, became weak like their enemies because the Spirit of the Lord no longer preserved them; it had withdrawn, for it “doth not dwell in unholy temples.” Samson’s words to Delilah, that shaved he would be weak and like any other man, and the narrator’s note that the LORD had departed, describe the same kind of loss.

Gives Samson as an example of measure for measure: he went after his eyes, so the Philistines put out his eyes (v. 21). In the same list Absalom, proud of his hair, is caught by his hair, so the two stories of hair and downfall are read side by side.

Rabbi Judah the Prince says Samson’s fall began in Gaza (v. 1), where he went to a harlot without marrying her, so it was fitting that he was blinded and imprisoned in Gaza (v. 21). He adds that even if she had not been called Delilah, the name would fit, from a verb for weakening: she weakened his strength, his heart, and his deeds. How did she know the fourth answer was true? Abaye says she knew Samson was righteous and would not use God’s name in vain, and this time he said he was a Nazarite “unto God.”

A baraita says Samson’s shoulders were sixty cubits across, since the gates of Gaza he carried off (v. 3) were held to be that wide. Rav hears in v. 28 a plea for unpaid service: remember the years I judged Israel, the Talmud counts twenty-two, without asking anyone even to move a stick for me. Among five men struck in the very gift they were known for, it lists Samson, struck in his strength (v. 19).

The Aramaic translation calls the woman at Gaza an innkeeper (v. 1), the word it also uses for Rahab (Joshua 2:1). Josephus likewise has Samson take lodging at an inn in Gaza and says nothing of a harlot there, though he calls Delilah one. Both readings move the judge’s first night at Gaza away from the plain sense of the Hebrew.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on Judges 16:1; Josephus, Antiquities 5.8.10

traditions.text: Josephus begins Samson’s ruin when he “transgressed the laws of his country” and took up foreign ways. At the feast the roof rested on two pillars, and Samson told the boy who led him that he was tired and wanted to rest against them. Josephus closes with a verdict: Samson deserves admiration for his courage, his strength, and his greatness of mind at his death; being ensnared by a woman belongs to human nature, and in all else he was a man of extraordinary virtue.

Sets the gate story at Azotus (Ashdod), where Samson calls the Philistines fleas, uses one gate as a shield and the other as a weapon. God himself foretells the fall: Samson has been led astray by his eyes and has forgotten Joseph, who kept himself in a strange land, so he will be blinded, yet in his death God will remember him. Delilah, here his wife, makes him drunk before the barber comes, and his last prayer adds, “Go forth, O my soul, and be not grieved.”

The writer to the Hebrews names Samson with Gideon, Barak, and Jephthah among those of whom there is no time to tell. The deeds he goes on to list include some that fit Samson’s story, such as those who “out of weakness were made strong.” The list says nothing of his failures.

Arguing that no one may lawfully take his own life, Augustine has to account for Samson, who pulled the house down on himself. He allows one defense only: the Spirit who worked wonders through Samson had secretly commanded him to do it. He sets the case beside soldiers acting under lawful command and Abraham’s readiness to sacrifice Isaac, and raises the same question about Jephthah’s daughter.

Ambrose reads the end as a triumph: in death Samson conquered himself and despised the death all men fear, and he was buried not by weapons but by the bodies of his enemies. Following Josephus closely, he puts the snare of a woman down to human nature more than to the man. The letter ends on its purpose, that “alliances with strangers should be avoided.”

Ambrose asks whether hair really held Samson’s strength and answers no; it was the grace of the Spirit, which left him on the knees of a woman. The hair stands for the faith and devotion of the Nazarite, and he links it to the head that is Christ (1 Corinthians 11:3). Yet he grants that Samson himself spoke plainly: shorn, his strength would go.

17.overview:
Micah, a man of the hill country of Ephraim, admits to his mother that he took the eleven hundred shekels of silver she had cursed the thief over. She blesses him and has two hundred shekels cast into a graven image and a molten image. Micah already keeps a house of gods with an ephod and teraphim, and makes a son its priest. Then a young Levite from Bethlehem-judah, looking for anywhere to settle, comes by. Micah hires him for ten shekels a year, clothes and food, and is sure the LORD will now do him good.

Watch the name. In vv. 1 and 4 he is *Mikayehu*, “Who is like the LORD?”, and he builds the LORD a shrine from stolen silver and forbidden images, with a priest for hire. The narrator's only comment comes in v. 6: there was no king, and every man did what was right in his own eyes.

17.hermeneutics:
Micah's offer in v. 10 can be priced. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) set a hired day laborer's wage at six grains of silver a day for the first five months of the year and five a day for the rest (§273), at 180 grains to the shekel. Over a year that comes to about eleven shekels. Ten shekels a year, a suit of clothes and food is the keep of an ordinary hired man, not the endowment of a sanctuary. The chapter uses the language of hire on purpose: the Levite is “content” (v. 11), and he later describes the arrangement in one word, “hired” (18:4).

Metal cult images were at home in these hills. In 1977 a bronze bull about 17.5 cm long was found on a ridge in the northern Samaria hills, and Amihai Mazar's excavations there (1978 and 1981) showed it belonged to a small walled open-air shrine of the 12th century BC, with a standing stone by its entrance. The site lies in the territory the Bible assigns to Manasseh; whether its builders were Israelites is debated. A “molten image” in a household shrine (v. 4) was the kind of object hill-country villagers really made, which is why the law curses “the man that maketh any graven or molten image” (Deuteronomy 27:15). Micah's mother pronounces her curse over the theft and none over the image.

notes: **Silver:** the Hebrew word comes seven times (vv. 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 10), carrying the story from the stolen hoard to the Levite's wage.

**Two consecrations:** Micah “consecrated” (literally, filled the hand of) a son in v. 5 and the Levite in v. 12. The Levite becomes “as one of his sons” (v. 11) and is also asked to be a “father” (v. 10).
**The LORD's name:** it appears three times (vv. 2, 3, 13), always in the mouths of Micah and his mother. The narrator himself calls the shrine a “house of gods” (v. 5).

Chapters 17–21 are the book's epilogue: no judge appears, and the refrain “no king in Israel” runs through it (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). Ch. 17 sets up ch. 18, where the Danites carry off Micah's images and his priest. Both stories of the epilogue open with a Levite and Bethlehem-judah (17:7; 19:1).

**Back:** Deuteronomy 12:8 forbids worship where every man does “whatsoever is right in his own eyes.” **Forward:** Ruth, the next book, also opens with a man of Bethlehem-judah going to sojourn (Ruth 1:1).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to “graven image” in v. 3 points to Abinadi reciting the commandment to the priests of King Noah: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image.” The link is apt beyond the words. Noah, too, had set aside the priests of his father's day and consecrated new ones of his own choosing (Mosiah 11:5).

As a thematic link, the Lord's preface to the Doctrine and Covenants describes a people in the same state as v. 6. They do not seek the Lord to establish his righteousness; instead “every man walketh in his own way,” after the image of his own god, an idol that will perish. Judges makes the point with a story about an actual image. The revelation applies the same description to the latter days, when the idol people follow is made in the likeness of the world itself.

This retelling gives Micah's mother a name, Dedila, and makes her the instigator: she urges him to melt down his gold and make gods, so that he will have a name, an altar and a paying business in sacrifices and incense. He makes images of three boys, calves, a lion, an eagle, a dragon and a dove. Each one answers a different request: the dove for wives, the boys for sons, the eagle for riches, the lion for strength, the dragon for long life.

God then speaks against Micah's images commandment by commandment. Israel had promised at Sinai not to make idols, not to take his name in vain, to keep the Sabbath, to honor parents, and not to steal, kill, commit adultery, bear false witness or covet, and the images, he says, break every one. Micah is sentenced to be burned and his mother to waste away before him, with worms coming from her body, a sentence the book reports carried out after the war on Benjamin (47:12).

The Aramaic translation reads the shrine as idolatry throughout. Micah's “house of gods” becomes a house of idols, and both his son and the Levite are called by the word for an idol-priest. In v. 13 the Targum makes Micah condemn himself in his own boast: the LORD will do him good, since he has a Levite as an idol-priest.

The Talmud asks why Micah is not listed among those who lose their share in the world to come, since he made idols that Israel worshiped. The answer is that his bread was open to every traveler who passed. When the ministering angels wanted to drive him out, God told them to leave him alone for that reason.

The Talmud takes up the puzzle of v. 7, a Levite “of the family of Judah.” One suggestion is that his father was a Levite and his mother from Judah; another, that he was a man of Judah whose name happened to be Levi, which Micah took as a lucky sign. The conclusion is that he was a true Levite, called “of Judah” because he acted like Judah's idolatrous king Manasseh, the same reason the Talmud gives for the name in 18:30.

A scribe must not erase a holy name, so the rabbis had to decide which divine names in chs. 17–18 are holy. The ruling: wherever these chapters say “God” (*Elohim*), the word is profane and means Micah's idol, while “the LORD” is holy. One exception is made, “the house of God” at Shiloh in 18:31.

This early chronicle places Micah's image and the crime at Gibeah in the days of Cushan-rishathaim, the first oppressor, when Othniel judged (3:8–11). Rashi gives the reasons: the image stood “all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh” (18:31), which covers the earliest years, and in 19:12 Jerusalem is still a foreign city, though Judah took it in Othniel's generation. The book has set these stories last for their meaning, not because they happened last, and Josephus also tells the war at Gibeah before any of the judges.
traditions.cite: Seder Olam Rabbah 12; Rashi on Judges 17:1

traditions.text: Rashi notes that some identified Micah's mother with Delilah, since both stories involve eleven hundred pieces of silver (16:5). He rejects the idea, because Micah lived many years before Samson. The stories sit side by side, he says, because the same sum of silver did harm in both.

18.overview:
The tribe of Dan, still without a settled inheritance, sends five men north to spy out land. Lodging at Micah's house, they recognize the young Levite's voice, and he gives them a favorable answer from God. At Laish they find a quiet, unguarded people with no allies, and they report back. Six hundred armed Danites set out, stop at Micah's house, and carry off his images, ephod and teraphim; the Levite goes gladly when offered a whole tribe instead of one household. Micah chases them and is threatened into turning back. The Danites put Laish to the sword, burn it, rebuild it as Dan, and set up the image.

Notice that the priest has no name until the last verses. In v. 30 the hired Levite becomes Jonathan son of Gershom, and the Church's footnote explains that “Manasseh” there was altered from Moses, Gershom's father (Exodus 2:22). The grandson of the lawgiver is serving a carved image.

18.hermeneutics:
Laish had once been part of a long trade network. A tin inventory from the palace of Mari on the Euphrates, from the reign of Zimri-Lim (18th century BC), lists tin sent west: thirty minas to Ibni-Addu, king of Hazor, and eight and two-thirds minas to Wari-taldu at Laish. Tin was what bronze-smiths could not do without, and Laish sat on the road that brought it. The Danites' spies find the opposite of that old connectedness: a people “far from the Zidonians” who “had no business with any man” (vv. 7, 28). The narrator stresses it because it means no one will come to help.

Late Bronze Laish was wealthy and faced the coast. In 1969 a built tomb at Tel Dan, Tomb 387, yielded gold and silver jewelry, bronze swords, ivory cosmetic boxes, and imported Mycenaean pottery, including a krater painted with chariots of a type most common on Cyprus. It dates to the 14th–13th centuries BC. That suits a town living “after the manner of the Zidonians” (v. 7), in the orbit of the Phoenician trading cities rather than the Israelite hill country.

The chapter's last note dates its writer. About 733–732 BC Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria annexed the north of Israel; his inscriptions claim the “wide land of Naphtali,” and 2 Kings 15:29 lists the upper Jordan towns whose people he deported. Dan stood at the head of that valley. Read this way, “until the day of the captivity of the land” (v. 30) means Jonathan's line served at Dan for centuries, until Assyria emptied the region.

notes: **The inventory:** graven image, molten image, ephod and teraphim are listed together in vv. 14, 17 and 18. The priest carries three of them in v. 20, and in vv. 30–31 only the graven image is set up. Micah's own name for them is “my gods which I made” (v. 24).
**Quiet and secure:** Laish is “quiet and secure” twice (vv. 7, 27) and “secure” once more in the spies' report (v. 10). The people are described more fully than the attack, which takes half a verse.
**Two dates:** v. 30 measures Dan's priesthood to “the captivity of the land,” v. 31 to the years God's house stood at Shiloh.

Ch. 18 completes the Micah story begun in 17:1, and its opening repeats “no king in Israel” (v. 1; 17:6). It fills out what Joshua 19:47 reports in one verse and resolves Judges 1:34, where the Amorites forced Dan into the hills.

**Forward:** Dan's shrine had a long future. Jeroboam set one of his golden calves there (1 Kings 12:29–30), and the tribe's migration explains why “from Dan even to Beer-sheba” (20:1) can mean the whole land.

traditions.text: Josephus tells Dan's migration with no Micah, no images and no Levite. In his version the Canaanites, with chariots and allies from Askelon and Ekron, drove the Danites into the mountains, so they sent five men who found good land near Mount Libanus and the springs of the lesser Jordan. He opens the story by saying that Dan suffered “in like manner with the tribe of Benjamin,” and places the move right after the war on Benjamin and before Othniel. A history written for Greek and Roman readers had no room for an Israelite shrine with a carved image and a grandson of Moses as its priest.

This retelling also drops the Danites and their migration entirely, moving straight from Micah to the Levite of ch. 19. Micah keeps his images in his own house until God punishes him, and after the war on Benjamin he is burned with fire while his mother wastes away, as God had said. Like Josephus, the author seems to have found the theft of the shrine not worth retelling.

The Danites' three questions in v. 3 (who brought you here, what are you doing, what have you here) are heard as echoes of words spoken to Moses, as if to ask whether a descendant of Moses would serve an idol. Jonathan answers with a saying from his grandfather's house: a man should hire himself out to idol worship rather than depend on charity. The Talmud says he misread it; the saying meant work that feels foreign to you, however lowly.

The same passage gives Jonathan a later life. When David saw how much he loved money, he made him overseer of the temple treasuries, and the Talmud identifies him with “Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses” in Chronicles. Rabbi Yohanan explains the new name as *shav la-El*: he returned to God with all his heart. The Talmud thus gives the priest of Dan's idol a story of repentance that Judges never tells.

In the Hebrew of v. 30 the *nun* of “Manasseh” is written above the line. Rashi, following the Talmud, says the letter was added out of respect for Moses, turning his name into Manasseh, and hung above the line to show that the name is really Moses. For the end of the verse Rashi names the exile under Sennacherib, which he counts as the first exile of the land.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Judges 18:30; b. Bava Batra 109b

traditions.text: The Aramaic keeps “Manasseh” but calls Jonathan and his sons idol-priests, the word it used for Micah's son. In v. 6 it has the Levite's answer come “through the Memra of the Lord,” smoothing over the fact that he was consulting images. At the end of v. 30 it makes the exile a deportation of people: Jonathan's sons served until the land's inhabitants were carried off.

A baraita in the name of Rabbi Natan measures the distance from Micah's town, Gerav, to Shiloh at three *mil*, about three miles. The smoke of the altar at Shiloh and the smoke of Micah's idol rose and mingled, the ministering angels wanted to push Micah away, and God held them back. The point picks up v. 31, where the stolen image and God's house at Shiloh stand in the same years. The rabbis took the closeness literally: two altars within sight, and no one in Israel objected.

On v. 5 Rashi says the Danites asked the Levite to inquire by the figurines, which spoke by sorcery. He reads the reply of v. 6, “before the LORD is your way,” as a hedge: the matter is known to God, and the figurines are worth nothing. On v. 29 he explains why Joshua calls the city Leshem: the Danites found there the precious stone *leshem*, the stone of Dan on the high priest's breastplate, and took it as a sign the land was theirs.

Jerome's Latin translation reads v. 30 as “Jonathan the son of Gersam the son of Moses,” with no Manasseh at all. He translated from the Hebrew, so he evidently read past the raised letter to the name written underneath it. The Douay-Rheims English, made from the Vulgate, kept Moses, and Western readers who used the Latin Bible met the name without any hint of the scribal change.

19.overview:
A Levite from the hills of Ephraim goes to Bethlehem to bring back his concubine, who has gone home to her father. Her father keeps him feasting four days and most of a fifth. Leaving late, the Levite refuses to stop at Jebus, a foreign city, and reaches Gibeah of Benjamin at sunset, where only an old man from Ephraim takes them in. At night men of the town surround the house and demand the guest. The host offers his virgin daughter and the concubine; the Levite seizes the concubine and puts her outside, and the men rape her all night. At dawn she falls at the door with her hands on the threshold. He tells her to get up, gets no answer, carries her home, cuts her body into twelve pieces, and sends them through Israel.

Notice that she never speaks. Father, servant, husband, host and mob all talk; when he finally speaks to her, “none answered” (v. 28).

19.hermeneutics:
Sending pieces of a body around the country was a known way to call men to arms. A letter to Zimri-Lim, king of Mari (18th century BC, ARM 2.48), complains that the Hanean tribesmen are slow to gather for a campaign. The writer proposes executing a prisoner, cutting off his head, and carrying it around the villages so the men will be afraid and assemble quickly. Saul later summons Israel with the pieces of a yoke of oxen, adding the threat in words (1 Samuel 11:7). The Levite's twelve pieces (v. 29) are a summons as much as an accusation, and they work: in 20:1 the whole nation gathers “as one man.”

Gibeah is usually placed at Tell el-Ful, about three miles north of ancient Jerusalem. W. F. Albright dug there in 1922–23 and Paul Lapp in 1964, finding a small Iron Age I settlement later replaced by a fortress, often linked with Saul; some scholars prefer Jaba', farther north. The distances make the Levite's choice clear. At dusk he was beside Jebus, a Canaanite town, and walked on about an hour rather than turn aside into “the city of a stranger” (v. 12), expecting safety among his own people. Gibeah is where the danger was.

notes: **Where the panels break:** at Sodom heaven intervenes; at Gibeah no one does. The LORD is named once in the chapter, in the Levite's own words, “the house of the LORD” (v. 18).

**Lodging and heart:** the verb “lodge” comes 11 times in vv. 4–20, and “heart” 6 times, from the Levite's errand to “speak friendly” (literally, to her heart) in v. 3 to the men of Gibeah making their hearts merry in v. 22.
**The verb of v. 29:** “divided” is the word for cutting up a sacrificial animal (Leviticus 1:6, 12; 1 Kings 18:23).

Ch. 19 opens the second story of the epilogue (19:1–21:25): the crime at Gibeah, the war on Benjamin, and the search for wives. Like ch. 17 it begins with “no king in Israel,” a Levite, and Bethlehem-judah (v. 1). The cry that ends it, “consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds” (v. 30), is answered by the assembly at Mizpeh in 20:1–7.
**Forward:** Gibeah becomes the home town of Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:26). **Back:** Genesis 19, whose wording the chapter borrows.

traditions.text: The prophet uses the night at Gibeah as a byword for the depths of Israel's sin: “They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah.” The Church's footnote at v. 14 points to the verse. In 10:9 he goes further and dates Israel's sin from the days of Gibeah, as though the nation's trouble began that night. Hosea is the earliest witness outside Judges that the story was known and remembered in the north, two centuries or more before the book reached its final form.

The Hebrew of v. 2 says the concubine “played the whore against him,” and early translators were not sure what to make of it. One major Greek manuscript, Codex Alexandrinus, says she was angry with him, while Codex Vaticanus says only that she went away. The Targum has her treat him with contempt, and Rashi reads the verb as leaving, going out from his home. Josephus (next entry) turns it into a quarrel, so that in most early readings she is not an adulteress at all.
traditions.cite: Judges 19:2 (LXX A and B); Targum Jonathan and Rashi on 19:2

traditions.text: Josephus makes it a story of an unhappy marriage: the Levite loved his beautiful wife, she did not love him, and after constant quarrels she went home until he came to make peace. The young men of Gibeah want the woman, not the man, having seen her in the market place. At dawn, he says, she reached the house and, ashamed, “durst not look her husband in the face,” and died. Her husband first thought she was asleep and tried to comfort her, since she had been taken by force.

This retelling moves the crime from Gibeah to Nob and names the Levite Beel and his host Bethac, a fellow Levite who warns him and prays that God will shut the townsmen's hearts as he did at Sodom. The men threaten to burn them all, drag out the man and his concubine, let him go, and abuse her until she dies. The author explains her death as punishment: she had once sinned against her husband with the Amalekites, so God gave her into the hands of sinners. Pseudo-Philo reads the Hebrew of v. 2 at its harshest, where the Greek and Aramaic soften it.

Why did she leave? Rabbi Evyatar says her husband found a fly in his food; Rabbi Yonatan says a hair. Evyatar asks Elijah what God says about it, and Elijah answers that God quotes both, calling each “my son,” because both are words of the living God. The Talmud then harmonizes them: he let the fly pass, but the hair made him lose his temper, and the passage became a classic lesson that two readings of one verse can both be kept.

From the same passage Rav Hisda draws a rule for households: a man should never impose excessive fear on his family. The husband of the concubine at Gibeah did, the Talmud says, and it led to the deaths of tens of thousands in Israel. The rabbis read the chapter as beginning with a man's temper, not only with the townsmen's crime. Rav adds that a frightened wife may run from home and into danger, which is what this story shows.

Commenting on Abraham's offer of a morsel of bread to his guests (Genesis 18:5), Rabbi Yitzhak finds the same phrase in all three parts of Scripture: in the Torah, in the Prophets with the father-in-law's “comfort thine heart with a morsel of bread” (v. 5), and in the Psalms (104:15). The midrash puts the Bethlehem father beside Abraham as a model of hospitality. The chapter itself draws the contrast: the father cannot let his guest go, and in Gibeah no one will take him in until an outsider from Ephraim does.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose retells the chapter to show how highly Israel once prized chastity. He guesses she was called a concubine from *concubitus*, sharing a bed, and describes the father-in-law delaying them out of affection. Dying at the door, he says, she was “guarding the feelings of a good wife” to the end, keeping at least her body for her husband. Where Pseudo-Philo blames her, Ambrose honors her, and he lays the guilt wholly on the men of Gibeah.

20.overview:
Israel gathers at Mizpeh “as one man,” four hundred thousand swordsmen from Dan to Beer-sheba. The Levite tells what happened at Gibeah, and the tribes swear not to go home until it is punished. Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men and musters 26,700, among them seven hundred left-handed slingers. Israel asks God who should go first and is told Judah. Benjamin wins twice, killing 22,000 and then 18,000. After weeping, fasting and sacrifices before the ark, where Phinehas serves, the LORD promises victory. An ambush takes Gibeah, a column of smoke signals the main army, and 25,000 Benjamites die. Six hundred escape to the rock of Rimmon; Israel puts Benjamin's towns, people and animals to the sword and burns them.

Notice that the LORD tells Israel to go up all three times. Forty thousand fall in obedience to his answers before the third answer adds “to morrow I will deliver them” (v. 28).

20.hermeneutics:
The sling was no boy's toy. Assyrian reliefs of the siege of Lachish (701 BC) show slingers ranked behind the archers, and smooth stones the size of a fist turn up in quantity at sites across the region. A trained slinger could hit hard at long range. Benjamin's seven hundred who could “sling stones at an hair breadth” (v. 16) explain how a small tribe could twice defeat an army many times its size from the walls and slopes of its own town.

Hill-country armies passed messages by fire. Lachish Letter 4, written about 588 BC as the Babylonians closed in, ends with an officer telling his commander that they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish, since they can no longer see Azekah. Jeremiah 6:1 tells the “children of Benjamin” to raise a sign of fire, the same Hebrew word as the “flame” of vv. 38 and 40. The ambushers' pillar of smoke was a prearranged signal to the main army (v. 38), and the Benjamites saw it only when they looked back.

In 1930 Martin Noth proposed that Israel's twelve tribes formed a sacred league around one sanctuary, like the Greek amphictyonies. The best known, the league of peoples around Delphi, fought sacred wars against its own members, Kirrha (596–585 BC) and Phocis (356–346 BC). Most scholars now doubt that Israel had so formal a league, but the comparison fits what this chapter shows: tribes acting together before God against one of their own.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, three battles each preceded by an inquiry of the LORD.
notes: **Rising cost of asking:** the first inquiry is a question (v. 18); the second adds weeping until evening (v. 23); the third adds fasting, burnt offerings and peace offerings (v. 26).
**Told twice:** the third battle is summarized in vv. 29–35 and told again in detail from v. 36, with Benjamin's boast “as at the first” (vv. 32, 39).
**Brother and sword:** Israel calls Benjamin “my brother” as it goes to war (vv. 23, 28). “Drew sword” comes six times (vv. 2, 15, 17, 25, 35, 46), counting both armies by the same measure.

Ch. 20 is the middle of the Gibeah story (19:1–21:25). The crime of ch. 19 brings the assembly, and the war's outcome, a tribe reduced to six hundred men (v. 47), creates the problem of ch. 21. Israel's demand to “put away evil from Israel” (v. 13) uses Deuteronomy's formula for executing a capital crime (Deuteronomy 17:12; 22:22).
**Forward:** Saul, Israel's first king, will call himself a Benjamite “of the smallest of the tribes” (1 Samuel 9:21).

traditions.text: Josephus has the elders hold back the angry tribes at first. Their law, he says, forbade making war even on foreigners without first sending envoys to see whether the offenders would repent. Only when Gibeah refused to hand over the young men, boasting it was no one's inferior in war, did Israel take up arms. In his telling the oath not to give daughters to Benjamin is sworn at this point, before the first battle.

His numbers differ from the Hebrew: Benjamin fields 25,600 men, of whom five hundred are left-handed slingers, and Israel loses only two thousand on the first day before night stops the fighting. After the second defeat the army goes to Bethel, fasts, and asks God through Phinehas the high priest. In the end the six hundred survivors break out in a close body and hold a mountain.

This retelling says outright what the chapter leaves unexplained. God answers “Go up” but deceives Israel, and they lose 45,000 and then 46,000 men. Phinehas, tearing his clothes before the ark, asks God what this deceit means, and reminds him of his own zeal against Zimri (Numbers 25), for which God had defended him.

God answers Phinehas with a parable. A lion set to guard the forest stayed silent while other beasts devoured the young, then roused the whole forest to war when one whelp of an evil beast was killed, and the beasts killed the lion first. So Israel, God says, stayed silent while Micah's images led them astray but rose up for the dead concubine; he let them fall, and now he will give them Benjamin.

The Talmud gives the same reason without the parable. Israel lost forty thousand men in the first two battles because of Micah's idol. God said to them, in effect: you did not protest for my honor, but you protest for the honor of flesh and blood. Pseudo-Philo and the Talmud, separated by centuries, read chs. 17 and 19–20 together in the same way.

The rabbis held that an answer of the Urim and Thummim could never fail, so they had to explain the two defeats. Their answer: the first two times Israel asked only how and whether to go to battle, not whether it would win. Only the third time, when Phinehas asked “or shall I cease?”, did the oracle answer about victory, and that answer came true.

A dispute over whether the divine names of ch. 20 are holy, and so may not be erased by a scribe, turns on the same puzzle. Rabbi Eliezer says they are not: the tribes were consulting an idol, for God does not promise and then fail. Rabbi Yehoshua says they are holy, since God answered exactly what was asked, and the last time Israel asked whether it would win.

Rashi works through the chapter's numbers. Benjamin mustered 26,700 (v. 15); 25,100 fell (v. 35) and 600 escaped (v. 47), which leaves a thousand men unaccounted for. He concludes that they fled to the towns and died the next day, when Israel turned on the cities of Benjamin (v. 48). He also takes Baal-tamar (v. 33), “lord of the palm,” as a pointer toward Jericho, the city of palm trees.

Describing the pilgrimage of his friend Paula through the Holy Land, Jerome says she stopped at Gibeah, then a ruin, remembering its sin and the concubine cut in pieces. She remembered too that a remnant of Benjamin was saved, so that in later days Paul could be called a Benjamite. Jerome gives the survivors as three hundred, not the six hundred of v. 47. Paul names his tribe in Romans 11:1 and Philippians 3:5, so for Jerome the near-extinction of Benjamin led, in the end, to the apostle.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose treats the war as proof of how highly Israel once valued chastity: forty thousand men drew the sword against their brothers to avenge one woman. Beaten at first, they would not give up, and he counts sixty-five thousand dead on both sides. He reads the defeats as the price Israel accepted, ready to wash out the stain of the crime with its own blood. Where the rabbis and Pseudo-Philo look for Israel's hidden sin, Ambrose praises its persistence.

21.overview:
At Bethel Israel weeps that a whole tribe is now missing. They have sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin, and they have also sworn death on anyone who failed to come to Mizpeh. Jabesh-gilead sent no one, so twelve thousand men go to kill its people, men, married women and children, sparing four hundred young virgins for Benjamin's survivors. Two hundred men still lack wives. The elders tell them to hide in the vineyards at Shiloh's yearly feast and seize girls who come out to dance, and promise to talk the fathers out of complaining. The Benjamites do it and rebuild their towns.

Watch the oath. Israel keeps its word not to give daughters to Benjamin (vv. 1, 7, 18) by destroying one town and arranging the abduction of girls from another. The narrator adds only the book's last line: there was no king, and every man did what was right in his own eyes.

21.hermeneutics:
Jabesh-gilead lay across the Jordan in Gilead. Its name survives in the Wadi al-Yabis, which runs down to the Jordan valley, and the town is usually placed at Tell el-Maqlub on the wadi, or else at Tell Abu al-Kharaz near its mouth; both were occupied in the Iron Age. Eusebius, writing in the early 4th century, put it six miles from Pella on the road to Gerasa. From there the men of Jabesh would have had to come down, cross the river and climb into the hills of Benjamin to reach Mizpeh. The oath of v. 5 made no allowance for distance: a town that did not come was to die.

An oath sworn at a muster bound everyone present under a curse. In a Hittite ritual for swearing in soldiers (CTH 427), the officiant melts wax and sinew in fire, shows the men a blind and deaf woman and women's clothing, and declares that whoever breaks the oath will melt, go blind, or be turned into a woman. Israel's oath at Mizpeh was of the same kind: “Cursed be he that giveth a wife to Benjamin” (v. 18), and death for any who stayed away (v. 5). An oath like that could not simply be dropped, and the chapter's two schemes are built to keep its words while undoing its effect: the girls of Jabesh come from a town that never swore, and the girls of Shiloh are not “given” but taken.
